utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Karnavas, are you ready for your cross argument -- for your closing argument? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's okay, Your Honour. It will be a closing and a cross. Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning Judge Argibay. Good morning, Judge Vassylenko. And as we normally start in the United States, may it please the Court. Hopefully it won't take all day. In a rush to judgement, in an agonising effort to justify a fait accompli the Prosecution conducted its investigation against Colonel Blagojevic, in my opinion, as a mere ceremonial detour to a predetermined end. The Prosecution, throughout its investigation, throughout its trial and unsurprisingly throughout its final brief has intractably refused to accept contradictory evidence, has relied at times on dubious, sometimes discredited sources and has clung protectively to its own though obviously erroneous conclusions while having reigned over an investigation with what I would call a haughty sense of infallibility. All this as it repeatedly and continually failed - and continues to fail - to assess accurately crucial evidence on crucial points of this case. Principally the Prosecution from the very start has been engaged in what I would call a faith-based investigation in which it applied investigative methods suffering from a severe case of group think. And by that I mean the Prosecution failed to test its initial assumptions that Colonel Blagojevic and the Bratunac Brigade must have been involved in the atrocities as one might quite naturally expect because of where Bratunac is located vis-a-vis Srebrenica. So that was a natural reaction. Programmed in this fashion, the OTP investigators, the in-house experts, if I may call them, the Prosecutors rejected any information, in my opinion, or evidence that did not support their thesis, their preconception, their initial assumption. In fact, whatever did corroborate their initial assumption, they exuberantly though blindly embraced with little regard to the creditability of the source --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We're going to hear your analysis and understandings of the evidence we have already admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I totally agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we are not doing an investigation on the behaviour of the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope you could concentrate on the evidence that we have already admitted rather than any attacks to your counterpart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can assure you that this is rather mild and watered down compared to what I would normally do in front of a jury,, but yesterday the Prosecution got up and expressed their views, their beliefs, what they thought. And in order for you, I believe, to dissect and understand their mental process, I need to at least establish what I believe is the theme and theory of our case, and our theory is that from the get-go, from day one, they indicted without investigating, and they indicted because of where the Bratunac Brigade was located and what they thought and what they continue to think, and what Mr. McCloskey said yesterday, that Colonel Blagojevic is the number three man. And I kind of found it rather surprising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm getting into that, Your Honour. So this is a little intro, if you may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's come to your theory of the case as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. And I'm going to tie all of this in, by the way, so it's not out there in the wind. As I said, I've watered it down as much as I can. It should come as no surprise that the Prosecution to have questioned or even doubted their initial assumption would have been nothing short of a heresy, which of course explains why the Prosecution, as I've indicated just now, in my opinion with result in mind at the outset indicted Colonel Blagojevic and only then conducted its investigation in order to shore up its initial beliefs, which is why I call it a faith-based investigation. Now, in your final brief we've laid out our theory of the case, although as you well know, Your Honours, we don't have to prove anything, it's not our burden. And over the next few sessions we will talk about the facts and what we believe them to be. Our theory in this case and what the evidence shows, Colonel Blagojevic was not involved in a joint criminal enterprise, was not involved in issuing any orders for any crimes to have been committed, did not turn a blind eye when he knew that his men were out there doing certain things, that the Bratunac Brigade was not out there committing crimes as the Prosecution would have us believe. We will try to bring in the other aspect, the one what is missing, the one that conveniently is tucked away or looked aside -- or not even considered. And of course we will be talking about the Prosecution's favoured truthful, cooperating witness, Momir Nikolic, who -- of course he is a member of the Bratunac Brigade and by virtue of his position we have to deal with, keeping in mind, of course, as I've indicated, that we have to examine him carefully and the Prosecutor said we need to take him with a grain of salt. I say we take him with a ton of salt. Because that man, as we saw, was all too willing to manufacture evidence - and I'm going to demonstrate how he did it - in order to sing the Prosecution's tune, because he knew what the tune was as it is laid out in the indictment, and he had all the evidence. So he had the music sheet. So all he had to do was tell what the Prosecution wanted to hear. And the Prosecution did not bother to check those facts, because to have checked them and perhaps to have found that those facts were anything other than what Mr. Nikolic was saying might have indicated that perhaps Mr. Nikolic was not quite as honest and Mr. Blagojevic was not quite as guilty or guilty at all. So -- now, the next section that I want to cover before I go into the facts -- and I'm going to apologise in advance for this. It's a little unusual, it's normally not my style. But I want to go into the law a little bit. In fact, I'm going to go into it a little bit longer than I want to with respect to complicity in genocide. I think it is necessary because I think this Tribunal is at a watershed. Because we're -- as I've indicated, and it's my firm belief, and it could be that I'm totally wrong I believe that aiding and abetting in genocide was not provided for in the statute but it is the law. It is the law. We must apply the law; I understand that. Now we've got this complicity in genocide, and we have to figure out where does it fit in and where is the mens rea. So I'm probably going to take the next 20 minutes in going over it. And I wanted to -- I'm a little more prepared than I was last time. And I want to factor in some of Mr. Shin's arguments, especially as it relates to Brdjanin. And before I begin, with respect to Brdjanin, let me say one thing, and I was a little troubled, because Brdjanin, as I read it, is pure dicta. Pure, unadulterated dicta. Why? Because it comes out and says there's no genocide. So once you find -- once you've established that, end of analysis. There's no need for you to go into is there complicity, can you have aiding and abetting in complicity. So it's pure dicta. Why that Trial Chamber decided to go into those matters, I don't know. Maybe it's because they want to be on the forefront, trailblazing, to see where we can stretch and broaden the horizon with respect to genocide and complicity in genocide, but nonetheless it's dicta. I raise this, and I'm kind of harping on it a little bit because in my jurisdiction if I was to raise dicta and not call it dicta, Judges would sanction me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to slandering of another Trial Chamber for no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nobody's slandering anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's exactly what's going on here. And the Prosecution is prepared to listen to this against us today, but another Trial Chamber, you know, that's just going too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think you have the right to air your views if you have different views with the decisions of another Trial Chamber, but you have to use the proper language and lay out your reasons and grounds. Let's concentrate on this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. But if I may remind the Court, the objection came as I was saying that it was dicta. I don't believe that that's slandering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. And I hope that the Prosecutor will restrain himself. All right. Now, first we have the Krstic appeal decision, which as I've indicated I believe that they've established a crime of aiding and abetting in genocide. Then Brdjanin comes along and in my opinion goes a little further than the Krstic appeal judgement. And it would appear, if you look at what they're saying, they're trying to create another crime or a new crime which would be aiding and abetting in complicity in genocide. Now, I want to focus on that and I'm going to be talking about that a little bit because if I listen to Mr. Shin correctly, I was under the impression yesterday as well as when I read his brief that we can have -- we can charge somebody with complicity in genocide and then there would be an A and a B. A where there's complicity with intent, and B where there's only knowledge. Maybe I have it wrong, but that's how I read it. Maybe they're saying there is a lesser included in complicity, although they don't say that. It might be implicit, I don't know. But that's what they're saying, and it's Brdjanin that they're relying on, hence why I'm going into this. Now, in their attempt to create this new crime, I believe, of aiding and abetting in complicity in genocide in Brdjanin, they state in paragraph 989 in dicta that -- they've already realised that there's no genocide. So we know this is dicta. At the outset I want to say that I believe the Krstic appeal judgement never really went into the issue of complicity in genocide to see whether -- what mens rea exists for that. It never really touched on it. They went around it a little bit. And perhaps because -- keep in mind that once they've realised that there was this aiding and abetting in genocide, there was no need for them to go to the next count, count 2, which would have been complicity. So one could say that that part of the Krstic appeals judgement is dicta. I'm not going that far; I don't believe it is. But I don't think they completed their analysis because they were more concerned in trying to figure out what the mens rea was for aiding and abetting in genocide, and I think there's pretty good language to establish that they believe that complicity in genocide is separate. Now, how does the Appeals Chamber come up with aiding and abetting? What was their reasoning? Well, as we know aiding and abetting is a mode of liability found in 7(1) which expressly applies to all crimes found in the statute. Because of the statute they indicated it must be read with the utmost respect of the language of the legislators. And the Appeals Chamber found that this was not an inadvertent overlap, so they looked at our statute. They cited the Stakic -- and I'm going to be discussing Stakic quite a bit. They cited the Stakic judgement which states that: "Complicity may encompass conduct broader than that of aiding and abetting." I'm going to stop right here and focus a little bit on one word and that is "conduct." So they're not talking about a mental element; it appears that they're talking about an actus reus, conduct. Then in Krstic they looked at four jurisdictions, the UK, France, Germany, and Switzerland that do not require a share intent for aiding and abetting for specific intent crimes but just knowledge. They have concluded that this was customary international law. Of course they didn't look at the other hundred or so jurisdictions. But it's interesting because of the one country they cite, UK, and I'm going to get to that. Now, I'm a little puzzled but the Appeals Chamber examined our statute and the legislators' intent, and there they said that in Article 4(2) spells out that the special intent required for all crimes enumerated in Article 4. Now, the first rule of statutory interpretation is to take the normal meaning of the statute on its face. So the Appeals Chamber actually states that Article 4 is: "Most naturally read to suggest that the Article 4(2) requirement that a perpetrator of genocide possesses the requisite intent to destroy. A protected group applies to all the prohibited acts enumerated in Article 4(3), including complicity in genocide." So it would appear, would it not - at least it does to me - that the Appeals Chamber acknowledges that the most natural reading of Article 4, that special intent is required for complicity in genocide and that there is no mention of aiding and abetting in Article 4. But let's go on. Let's look at the intent of the drafters of the statute. Since Article 4 was taken verbatim from the genocide convention, I believe we must look to the drafters of that convention. Now, surprisingly the Appeals Chamber in Krstic cited the travaux preparatoires - I hope my French is good enough to understand - of the genocide convention and actually stated, and I quote: "That the drafters of the genocide convention intended the charge of complicity in genocide to require a showing of genocidal intent." That's what comes from the convention. And it's interesting, because if we look at that, then we don't have to really go on any further with our analysis, but let's go on anyway. Because in the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement it went on to describe the Sixth Committee of the General Assembly where the UK delegate -- remember we talked about the UK, the one jurisdiction that they looked and they said that you only need knowledge. The UK delegate proposed adding the word "deliberate" before complicity, explaining that it was important to specify that complicity must be deliberate because there exists some systems where complicity required intent and others, such as in the UK, where it did not. Separate delegates representing Luxembourg, Egypt, the Soviet Union and, yes, Yugoslavia. They said that it was unnecessary because there had never been any doubt that complicity in genocide must be intentional. So the UK withdrew its amendment since it was understood that to be punishable, complicity in genocide must be deliberate. And of course I looked it up in Black's. No doubt in my mind that deliberate means intent. But there's a reason why I point to Black's and we'll get to that. Let's pause here with our analysis. Would you not agree that the statutory interpretation and the legislative intent would lead you to conclude that special intent is required for complicity in genocide? In any event, after making this pronouncement the Krstic Appeals Chamber then declined to tell us what the mens rea is for complicity in genocide where, and I quote: "Strikes broader than the prohibition of aiding and abetting." And I think this is an obvious sign that this judgement does not concern complicity. That's my interpretation. And of course when we get into Stakic, I think that might give us some guidance because I think - and I don't want to get ahead of my argument - but the real problem that they're having - I believe, and I'm not a legal scholar, I'm just a lawyer. Once they concluded that you have this aiding and abetting in genocide, the aiding and abetting conduct - the actus reus - and complicity are virtually the same, but you have two separate crimes. And what distinguishes them is the mens rea, the intent. Knowledge, special intent. Aiding and abetting in genocide, complicity in genocide. But I'm getting ahead of the story now. So let's look at the definition of aiding and abetting genocide. And I turn to the Stakic Trial Chamber, and it states that aiding and abetting in genocide is, in quotes: "All acts of assistance or encouragement that have substantially contributed to or have had a substantial effect on the completion of the crime of genocide." I notice that there's nothing in the definition that refers to the mens rea. Could it be that the Stakic Trial Chamber was simply opining on that complicity of aiding and abetting, complicity in genocide were the same, and it was not saying anything about the mens rea in complicity. I don't know. I wasn't there. I wish I had been a fly on the wall to see the discussion. But I'm reading the tea leaves and that's what it's telling me. Because they go on into the next paragraph and they say: "For the purpose in this case" - in the Stakic case - "the Trial Chamber deems it unnecessary to expand on the actus reus and the mens rea for complicity in genocide." And, again, I believe they did that because to have done anything other than that would have been dicta. Because in that case they found there wasn't any genocide, so they didn't go any further in their analysis. So where am I going with all this. The Krstic Appeals Chamber, it would appear, saw that sentence in the Stakic Trial Chamber decision and then used it to advance its reasoning in finding aiding and abetting genocide while not specifically opining on the mens rea for complicity in genocide. But now we're left with this appeals judgement from Krstic, so we need to look at that a little closer. And we see that the discussion of complicity seems, as I said earlier, almost incidental, subsidiary and possibly dicta, but I'm not quite sure. I've read it a few times. It's a little bit difficult, and I gather because there must have been a struggle to find the right balance, but I've never been a Judge, so I don't know what goes on and how they go about in making these decisions. But if you look at -- and I say this because first the conviction of General Krstic of aiding and abetting; therefore they didn't need to go into count 2, as I indicated, which would have been complicity. But the Krstic appeal states in paragraph 138: "Krstic's responsibility is accurately characterised as aiding and abetting genocide under Article 7(1) of the statute, not complicity as under Article 4(3)(e)." The Appeals Chamber is clearly keeping aiding and abetting genocide and complicity as two separate crimes. That's my interpretation of that. And that's where I think Brdjanin goes wrong. They say even though complicity can consist of aiding and abetting, what sets them apart is the level of intent. That's my opinion. What sets them apart is the level of intent. If you look at paragraph 142 of the appeals judgement, you see a discussion of the Sixth Committee of the General Assembly where it was unequivocally stated that complicity should require special intent. Then if you should look at the last sentence it says: "The text of the Tribunal statute and the genocide convention combined with the evidence in the conventions travaux preparatoires provide additional support to the conclusion that the drafters of the statute opted for applying the notion of aiding and abetting to the prohibition of genocide under Article 4," not complicity in genocide. They just say "genocide." And I think that's fairly relevant information, okay. So I think the whole discussion in Krstic was to incorporate aiding and abetting, which only requires knowledge into Article 4, under genocide, because it overlaps 7(1) in Article 4. Now, in doing that the Appeals Chamber realised that complicity and aiding and abetting, as I've indicated, have essentially the same actus reus, and this would no doubt create confusion to its proper charge. I mean, imagine if -- if I listened correctly to Mr. Shin yesterday, and I thought I did, it would seem that sometimes you could charge somebody, as I indicated, with complicity but you would mean intent but sometimes knowledge. And with charging somebody, there needs to be specificity; they need to know. So either inside complicity you can have A and B, or you have it as a lesser included. Then you must have as a lesser included aiding and abetting to incitement, to conspiracy, and what's a aider and abettor to a conspiracy? He's a co-conspirator. Automatically. End of analysis. That's why I think - if I have it right - this whole analysis of the Stakic and the Krstic and the Brdjanin they're really -- at least Stakic and Krstic are really talking about actus reus because there is this conundrum, how to solve it. Now, the Prosecution states that the Krstic Appeals Chamber holds that aiding and abetting is a part of complicity and only requires knowledge so that in this case under Count 1(B) Colonel Blagojevic should only be convicted of complicity in genocide because he only had knowledge to genocidal -- of the genocidal intent of others, if I'm stating their case correctly, and I believe I am. However, if you look at Judge Shahabuddeen's dissent he starts by agreeing with the majority in the Krstic with his brethren on Appeals Chamber that there is a crime of aiding and abetting the commission of genocide under customary international law. Now it's worth noting that Judge Shahabuddeen, who is meticulous in the way he writes. He says: "That the majority held that the crime is aiding and abetting the commission of genocide." "Aiding and Abetting the commission of genocide." Nothing about the commission of complicity in genocide. So I would think that surely we don't want to suggest that Judge Shahabuddeen had the majority's opinion wrong. So I think if you look at Judge Shahabuddeen's statement combined with the supporting material cited in Krstic, it clearly shows that aiding and abetting is part of genocide and not complicity in genocide. I know I'm a little long-winded, Your Honours, but I just need a little bit longer. I just want to make sure I nail this one down, and I think it's important, and I hope I'm being clear enough. Now, let's return to the Prosecution. They state that the Brdjanin Trial Chamber correctly followed the Krstic Appeals Chamber's holding that complicity in genocide under Article 4(3)(e) can consist of aiding and abetting genocide. Again, as I've stated earlier, the Prosecution failed to mention that this conclusion in Brdjanin was dicta, but nonetheless I have to mention it again. But for the sake of argument let's see how the Trial Chamber in Brdjanin reaches this conclusion. They begin their analysis of Article 4 by recognising that it was taken verbatim from the convention. All right, fair enough. However, it then says that: "Even though Article 4 does not contain command responsibility as a mode of liability, there are a play of factors that explain for this oversight." But then they don't tell us what those factors are. But based on that and the fact that Article 7(3) expressly applies for the crimes of the statute, the Trial Chamber concluded, without citing any authority, that command responsibility applies to Article 4 and that the commander need only have knowledge, not special intent. This was dealt with in Stakic. The Appeals Chamber cites this Rwandan case - I don't want to butcher the name, but it's C-y-a-n-g-u-g-u - which found a commander guilty of genocide under command responsibility for one incident. And then the Brdjanin Trial Chamber indicated that it disagreed with the Stakic Trial Chamber. And in my opinion, by diluting the mens rea for command responsibility, they went ahead and diluted the mens rea for complicity in genocide. The Brdjanin Trial Chamber began its analysis of complicity by stating that: "Complicity and accomplice liability have the same meaning." Then they turn to Black's Law Dictionary for that definition which is why I pointed it out as well. Because I think if Black's Law is good enough for that decision, Black's Law should be good enough to guide us as to what deliberate means. And deliberate means intentional, premeditated, fully considered. That's the definition in Black's. Now here's what's interesting in the Brdjanin Trial Chamber. They noted that the actus reus of complicity in genocide can consist of aiding and abetting. Well, as I said, that's axiomatic given that it's the same actus reus. Because it's not every conduct that amounts to complicity already amount to aiding and abetting. Of course. What separates them, as I said, is the level of intent. And Brdjanin cites Stakic for this conclusion and then qualifies Stakic by saying that there are -- "that there may be" - and I quote: "That there may be other acts which are not strictly aiding and abetting but which could amount to complicity." Here's where we're getting into some problems, because again we're talking about conduct, not mens rea. They then conclude that the: "Mens rea of complicity in genocide where it consists of aiding and abetting genocide does not require special intent." Let me read that again. "The mens rea of complicity in genocide where it consists of aiding and abetting genocide does not require special intent." But when does it consist of aiding and abetting? Well, let me go to -- let me see if I can figure this one out. Krstic says that there's a crime of aiding and abetting genocide. Brdjanin, in dicta, says: "Where it consists of aiding and abetting genocide does not require special intent." And we are in this case with a charge of complicity in genocide, so we have to figure out what is the proper actus reus and mens rea. And I don't think Brdjanin helps us. Not at all. Because in a footnote they proclaim that complicity and genocide are not, and I underscore, are not two distinct crimes, but rather they are different forms of a participation in the same crime." So here we see Brdjanin coming for the first time and saying that now complicity in genocide is part and parcel of genocide. It's a lesser included, at least that's my reading of it from that footnote. But if we seek some -- maybe if we seek refuge in Stakic, they may help us out, and I believe it will. Now, Stakic has this great analysis of Article 4. And I don't say this because we have two distinguished members of the Stakic Trial Chamber before us. First the Stakic Trial Chamber pointed out that Article 4 was taken verbatim from the statute. It then said that it was following the principle of non-retroactivity of substantive criminal law, which means the accused has the right to know what he is charged with. Of course. Given the principle of nullum crimen sine lege, the Stakic Trial Chamber looked at four sources when interpreting the crime of genocide. The convention, the object and purpose of the convention reflected in the travaux preparatoires, ICTY, ICTR, international court jurisprudence, international publications. Next, the Trial Chamber in Stakic adopted the description of genocide as the crime of crimes, which it is, it was meant to be, it has to be. It's a stigma. And they cited a -- the Kambanda case from ICTR. The Trial Chamber noted quite correctly, and I'm going to quote this: "Interpreting Article 4 restrictively and with caution will always be guided by the unique nature of the crime of genocide." By the unique nature of the crime of genocide. And those are the operative terms that missing both, by the way, in the Krstic and also in Brdjanin. But I think this is the guiding light, the compass that set the Stakic sails on the right course. Because now the Stakic trial says that genocide is a unique -- is so unique that it has the special intent, and then it goes on to say that the Prosecution when they submitted -- that the third category of the JCE did not require special intent, that was dismissed. And here's what the Trial Chamber had to say: "The application of a mode of liability cannot replace a core element of a crime." They want to keep things distinct. It goes on: "The Prosecution confuses modes of liability in crimes themselves." This is what the Trial Chamber said, so I'm not trying to disparage anybody. "Conflating the third variant of joint criminal enterprise in the crime of genocide will result in the dolus specialis being so watered down that it is extinguished." That's poetry as far as I'm concerned. Now, isn't that what the Prosecution is actually suggesting in this case? And if you look at the arguments that they made when they wanted to amend the indictment for the fourth or the fifth time, whatever it was, the Prosecution, they already had charged Colonel Blagojevic with genocide and in the alternative with complicity. They dropped genocide thinking that we'll go with complicity, still with a special intent. Krstic then comes out, as I have indicated, takes the wind out of their sails because now they see the writing on the wall. They try to go back to genocide but under a lesser included, according to Krstic, of aiding and abetting. That motion is denied in the interest of justice, as I recall those were the terms. So now they're saying, well, you know, actually in complicity in genocide you can have two types: One with intent, one with knowledge. And we want to go with knowledge right now. So that's their current position. Of course if that was their current position -- if their current position is correct, one has to wonder: Why put me through the meat grinder in having to file a response to their motion? Why waste our time over here? Why go through it if it's already in there? And I don't say this to be -- to demean anybody, but it's like a moving target for the Defence. What do we have to defend today? And that's what it feels like being on the receiving end. So let me move on, and I'll try to streamline it as much as I can. Stakic tells us that there's an overlap between 7(1) and 4(3)(e). Article 7(1) and Article 4(3)(e). It then adopted a finding from the Semanza Trial Chamber which said that: "There's no material distinction between complicity in genocide and the broad definition accorded to aiding and abetting," but we were not told what this broad definition is in Stakic. But it was correct, in my opinion, Stakic was correct in opining that the actus reus and the mens rea of complicity -- of not opining on the actus and mens rea because as I indicated that would have been dicta. So where are we? Well, thanks to Krstic we have this lesser included crime of genocide -- of aiding and abetting in genocide. But Colonel Blagojevic is not charged with genocide; he's charged with complicity in genocide which requires, in my opinion, and on the readings that I've indicated, the special intent. Now the Prosecution is asking you, in my opinion, to find a new crime of aiding and abetting in complicity in genocide. And we are left with this prevailing statement of complicity can consist of aiding and abetting. Complicity can consist of aiding and abetting. And this statement is found in Stakic and Krstic and Brdjanin. So what does it mean? Brdjanin and the Prosecution concluded that it means that aiding and abetting is a lesser included crime of complicity and only requires knowledge, that you can be charged with complicity in genocide and be convicted without special intent. I think if I understand their positions. But if you look at the statement, it says nothing about the mens rea element. I go back to mens rea because I think that's what we have to focus on. Now, let's look at the actual definition of aiding and abetting genocide. Krstic cites Stakic which defines it as all acts of assistance or encouragement that have substantially contributed to or have had a substantial effect on the completion of the crime of genocide. This is adopted by the Krstic Appeals Chamber and it must be followed, but let's examine it. First, aiding and abetting genocide is not part of complicity because the definition says: "Substantial effect to the crime of genocide." That's what they're saying: "Substantial effect to the crime of genocide," not substantial effect to the crime of complicity in genocide. Next. There's nothing in the definition describing the mens rea element, just the actus reus. And does not the actus reus sound the same as complicity in genocide? I think they do. And as I indicated what makes the difference is the intent. So that's how you get to aiding and abetting in complicity versus -- aiding and abetting in genocide versus complicity in genocide because they share the same actus reus, and that's why we need to have this distinction, plus if you look at the historical background. So in my opinion I would ask respectfully, and I apologise for taking so long, but I thought I needed to go through this explanation. I hope it has been informative, but I would ask you to essentially reject the Prosecution's argument with respect to complicity in genocide. I don't think in reading the indictment that they ever intended to charge with mere knowledge because they could have done that from the get go. Nothing stopped them, nothing prevented them. I don't think that we can look at the Brdjanin dicta at this point in time. We certainly don't want to be acting retroactively. And I think the Krstic judgement does not say that all you need is knowledge for complicity in genocide. We laid out our argument in our brief, and we think that it would be consistent with the Krstic appeal judgement if the Trial Chamber were to come out and say that for complicity in genocide, all the reasons that I've stated and perhaps a lot more than you can come up with, that you need the special intent, because that's what the drafters intended, and it's quite clear. And you see the UK, which is cited in the Appeals Chamber, the UK itself wanted to put the word "deliberate" in there, because of its own jurisdiction, its own laws, knowing that without that there may be some confusion. So I think it would be wholly consistent for you to go ahead and reject the Prosecution's argument and hold them to that standard, that for complicity in genocide it has to be the special intent. And again I apologise for taking all this time. I suspect there aren't any questions on this part, so I'll move on. Again, my apologies. That's probably more than Mr. Shin wanted to hear on complicity in genocide. Now I want to talk a little bit about probably my favorite doctrine, so-called doctrine, that we have in this Tribunal, and that's the doctrine of joint criminal enterprise. I call it the so-called doctrine because it appeared out of nowhere. We had common purpose during Nuremberg and during Tokyo. That didn't work very well. I think we all know that, we all realise it. It certainly is not in the statute. I looked for it; I couldn't find it. It came out of, as we all know, Tadic. And in my opinion, and I don't mean to disparage the Tadic case, but Tadic, I think, was sort of the midwife of a lot of law creating in this Tribunal, perhaps because it was the first case, and there was a lot of areas where there lacuna that needed to be filled. But it would seem to me that Tadic was - how should I say - very energetic in setting up different standards and laws. And from Tadic emerged this concept of joint criminal enterprise which is a real conundrum, I think, to Defence lawyers and to the courts. It certainly is not for the Prosecution because they tend to love that. It's based on this conspiracy model. Now, it's well settled that the JCE, and I'll refer to it as that, the joint criminal enterprise, the JCE, albeit being judicially created, that's my opinion but I think others agree with me, is part of the Tribunal's jurisprudence so we have to follow it. Whether we like it or not. Be that as it may, the Trial Chamber must not and should not interpret JCE to be a mere membership in an organisation because this would constitute most definitely a new crime not foreseen by the statute and would amount to an obvious infringement of the principle of nullum crimen sine lege. Now I mention that. You may say, well, wait a minute, why are you going -- where are you going with that? Well, you know, member of the VRS, and I'm going to tie it in, and we're going to go through my analysis but that's where I'm getting at. I'm not suggesting that that is the Prosecution's position, but I am suggesting that we are dangerously getting close there, not because of the Prosecution's intent but because of the nature of the beast, and the beast is the JCE. So, anyway, the Prosecution correctly set out the actus reus and the mens rea of the JCE and the separate categories of JCE, and in this case particularly we have 1 and 3. However, the Prosecution disagrees with the -- with a requirement that the Brdjanin Trial Chamber found that there must be an agreement between the accused and the physical perpetrators of the crime; they didn't like that part. Then they say that Brdjanin is distinguishable on the facts because the JCE in that case was in a large area over a long period of time. And so when I heard it I thought about it a little bit, and it would appear to me - and I don't know whether I'm correct or not - but it would appear that the Prosecution is suggesting that the JCE should be applied differently based on the facts of a case. I don't think that's correct. I think the law should be applied as is. Unless we're going to say we have different types of JCE, but that wasn't what we were hearing because that we have these three categories. It is worth noting that the two factors that led the Brdjanin Trial Chamber, and that might help us a little bit in this case. I assume I'm going to get some rebuttal on it. But what motivated Brdjanin to dismiss the JCE as a mode of liability is that they found that the accused was physically remote from the physical perpetrators and he did not have de facto authority over them. And when I talk about command responsibility, in essence that's what we're talking about, de facto. We can throw de jure out the window, in essence, because it really doesn't make a difference. It's de facto. You can have de jure and de facto, or just de facto, but de facto is what makes you responsible, in essence. But I'm going to talk about that, and I'll be very brief on that as well. They also indicated that they didn't like the Stakic definition of co-perpetration. They thought that was wrong. Well, I'll tell you what my opinion is with the JCE is that it creates a foggy and a rather dangerous impression of collective guilt. That's what I think. Where just because you are a member of an organisation or some members of that organisation went on to commit crimes or have committed crimes, your mere membership makes you liable. And -- or at least they look at your membership and then with all the circumstantial evidence they are able to say, you know, he must have known, he had to know, and somehow you're in this web where you have nothing to do with the enterprise, and what gets you into the web is your membership in the organisation. I think that's why continental Judges don't like this because they don't -- in the legal tradition, as I understand it, you have perpetrators and co-perpetrators, and that's it, in essence. And that's what we should be dealing with, as opposed to this theory that broadens the net and dangerously gets us close to what was happening at the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials. So in the example that I wanted to give you is that the Prosecution, throughout its final brief, uses the long-term objectives of the RS, the VRS to infer criminal or even, you know, the ethnic cleansing liability. Yesterday we heard the six stated goals, 1992. Think about it, and I'm going to talk about that. But it would appear, since that was out there in the open and that Colonel Blagojevic was a member of the VRS, there was a war going on, therefore we can look as far back as 1992 and then draw some inference as to what a state of mind is in 1995. And that's the danger. But what's even further, it would have been virtually impossible to have been a Bosnian Serb in Bosnia at that time and not to have known those stated goals. And if they were serving in the VRS, as they were, as they had to, at age 16, it would mean that once you turned 16 you became a member of this joint criminal enterprise. And that's the danger. I'm not saying that that's their argument -- that's their theory, but I'm saying that's how dangerous it can be when you apply this JCE. I do think that the Prosecution is misguided to even be suggesting the 1992 stated goals. Why do I say that? I'm going to get ahead of my argument, but I'm going to say it to just get it over with. If we're going to do that, then shouldn't the Defence not be allowed to question why you had these stated goals? What motivated the Serbs? It wasn't as if in 1992 they woke up and said, okay, let's ethnically cleanse Bosnia. It didn't happen. So you have to go back to the history. You have to go into the psyche of the Serbian people in Bosnia, which would require me to go into World War II, maybe the Ottoman Empire, stuff that is totally irrelevant in this case, and I don't want to make it part of this case. So as a Defence I'm in this straightjacket, and that straightjacket, in a sense, it has gotten tighter and tighter, thanks to you all, is called the indictment. Every time I try to get out of it, no, you're going to stick to that indictment. That's what you're going to defend. Once you had that 98 bis decision, that jacket got a little tighter. And so I have to tell you when the decision came out I thought, great. Then when I started putting on my case, I was wondering why are the Judges so much in a rush? Why are they cutting me off? Well, it wasn't that you were cutting me off. You were telling me - I hope - that your case is smaller, it's shrunk, focus on the indictment. I hope I was a good student and picked up and did what I was supposed to do. What I'm trying to get at is when you get to this JCE and you don't allow the Defence to go into it because it's irrelevant, but you bring it in somehow because it's this fuzzy thing called crime base. And I'll tell you, in 20 years I had never heard that word before. I had to come to The Hague to hear it for the first time. It seems it's a moving target too. It grows, it's hard to figure out what is and what isn't crime base; I know there's a definition. But from a Defence standpoint, maybe it's my training in front of juries because, you know, you never know where the jury is going to go, so you try to cover all bases. So you try to go off into the furthest stretch of their imagination, just in case they wander off the reservation. But I think the JCE causes that problem, and what we don't want to be is where others have been as a result of that. Now, where am I getting with all of this? Frankly I think that there must be a limit to the third category of the JCE based on a better way of interpreting co-perpetration pursuant to committing. Again, just by serendipity, not by design, I have to go to Stakic. And so the Stakic decision again gives us pretty clear guidance. They emphasise that: "JCE is only one of several possible interpretations of the term committing under 7(1) of the statute and that other definitions of co-perpetration must equally be taken into account." Fair enough. Furthermore, a more direct reference to committing in its traditional sense should be given priority. Now, why are they saying that? Because you have this JCE which is sort of, as I said, created outside the statute. Okay, there's some linkage because of the common purpose doctrine from Nuremberg and Tokyo. But basically the Stakic Trial Chamber is saying a more direct reference to committing in its traditional sense should be given priority. And they give the definition. It's on 439, I was prepared to read it, but I think we're losing time, so I don't want to take up too much more time. But what I am -- and I'm not suggesting that JCE should not be considered at all; that's not the purpose. But as I indicated, it's not the only definition. I believe that the Trial Chamber should consider the less confusing definition of committing that came out of the Stakic Trial Chamber. This definition provides a better understanding to that term and avoids the possible misleading impressions resulting from a wrongful application of this so-called doctrine of joint criminal enterprise. All right. And again, I apologise for having to do all this on the law, but I think for context purposes and because I think we are on the watershed of working with some of these concepts, fine-tuning them, I think it's important. And now I want to talk a little bit very briefly about the concept of command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that the interpreters have a very difficult time to follow you because first you delivered your argument in a very fast speed. Secondly, it's a very complicated issue. And my suggestion is that maybe we could have an early break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And after the break please keep your pace and we'll carefully listen to every word of your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Sleep deprivation makes me a little anxious, but yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll resume at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. And my deepest apologies to the translators. I'll try to go at a slower pace. I want to talk a little bit about command responsibility. And even though it's a sort of a well-known concept, recently we had a -- what I would consider a marvelous decision on this concept, the Blaskic decision. It sort of gives us a little bit more clarity on it. So I thought I would cover it just so we have some context. So as you know that under Article 7(3) command responsibility exists and the Celibici trial judgement more or less set the standard with the three-pronged test. The three-pronged test essentially is that, one, there must be superior support subordinate relationship between the superior and the perpetrators of the crime. So that's number one. Number two, the accused knew or had reasons to know that the crime was about to be or had been committed. And number three, the accused failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the crimes or punish the perpetrators thereof. So those are the basic three-pronged tests. So -- but I want to cover the Blaskic case a little bit in conjunction with how it talks or discusses the Celibici decision. So first we have to have this superior subordinate relationship, and there cannot be, in this relationship, unless, unless - and I cannot underscore this enough - there is an effective command and control over the subordinate. See, before I mentioned de jure and de facto, that's what that is all about. Effective command and control. Those are the operative words. Now, how do we know, how do we know, what is effective command and control? Well, we have this non-exclusive list that has been provided over the few years in the jurisprudence, and of course this concept came out of World War II during the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials that was covered. But here, you know, we have the superior -- de jure or de facto position of authority. That's important. That's one of the factors. His material ability to prevent or punish the commission of the crime. That's another factor. Again, these are non-exclusive but that's a factor. The actual influence he has over his subordinates. The actual influence he has over his subordinates. So if you have someone who doesn't want to stay on the porch and is roaming around on the prairie, say like Nikolic, well, do you have actual influence over him? We'll talk about that. But what Blaskic tells us is that it's a matter of evidence and not law. In other words, you can't just have this list. You look at it on a case-by-case basis. So each case you have to look at it for what it is. And what does that mean? Not evidence -- not law but evidence. Well, that these indicia, these indicators are indicia, not elements of effective command and control. They are just indicia. That these indicia must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis, and that these indicia are limited only - are limited only - to showing that the superior had the power to prevent or punish the commission of the alleged crime. So the Trial Chamber must, in my opinion, look at the specific facts of this case and this case alone to determine whether Colonel Blagojevic -- oh. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have a problem with the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can rewind, Your Honour. If I know where to pick up. I just have to push the button and I'll -- okay. Obviously they missed the part about being off the prairie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, it's not ready

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Are we on? All right. I can do it twice, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You know where you are?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was talking about if we had somebody, for instance, that left the porch and went off on the prairie. I was making reference to Nikolic, but we'll get there. But in any event just to make sure that the record is complete, what I indicated earlier was that it was a matter of evidence and not law. What that means is as follows: That these indicators that we spoke of are merely indicia, not elements of effective command and control. They help us to get there, to understand it, but they're not elements. That these indicia must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. That's very, very critical. So you can't look and see what they did in another case, you have to look at these facts. And perhaps if I may, you also have to look at the individual involved. That's where I may have some discussion with respect to what I heard yesterday because there was sort of a leap when Mr. McCloskey was saying, well, you know, Drago Nikolic and Obrenovic, they have this wonderful relationship. So it should follow that that's what was between Colonel Blagojevic and Momir Nikolic. So we'll talk about that. And that these indicia are limited only to showing, only to showing, that the superior had the power to prevent or punish the commission of the alleged crime. So this Trial Chamber must, in my opinion, look at the specific facts in this case and in this case alone to determine whether Colonel Blagojevic had effective command and control over the alleged perpetrators. Second, according to the Celibici Appeals Chamber, the Prosecutor must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the superior knew or had reasons to know that his subordinates were about to commit or had committed a crime beyond a reasonable doubt. And I'll share with you what my definition is of beyond a reasonable doubt just in case I forget it. In my jurisdiction, it is proof of such a convincing nature that you are willing to rely and act upon it without hesitation in your important affairs. And an important affair would be like getting married, for instance. So you don't go into marriage thinking, well, maybe it's the right person, maybe not, I don't know, maybe it will work. You're certain by that point. Or if you're going to buy a house or maybe even a car. And I mentioned that because at some point I might ask you whether you would be willing to buy a used car from someone like Nikolic based on his representations, because that's certainly not an important affair. So anyway. Now, certainly there are two kinds of knowledge that we all know that through the jurisprudence are recognised in trying to establish this effective command and control. You have the actual knowledge of the crimes which can be established through direct or circumstantial evidence, and I'll talk more about circumstantial evidence, and then you have constructive knowledge; that is, would have had reason to know. That's what they mean by that. Now, what does all of this mean? It means that the superior had in his possession information, had in his possession information, that would at least put him on notice of the present and real risk of such offence. To put it another way: "The Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the superior had either did actually know his subordinates committed the crime or that he would have known, given the information available to him." I think I'm accurately stating the law. Now, the Blaskic Appeals Chamber rejected criminal negligence as a basis of liability; you know, that he should have known. That was the test they used. They departed from Celibici. And in the Appeals Chamber, as you well know, they came back. And so negligence is not the standard, meaning that if a superior did not know of his subordinates' behaviour because of his own negligence, that that is not enough to satisfy the standard that he knew or had reasons to know. That's important. And I believe it comes very close -- as a result of what happened, I believe, in other cases during the Nuremberg or the Tokyo trial, the Yamashita case is the one that comes to mind where basically if you really want to cut to the chase after the war they -- the Supreme Court in the U.S. basically did not apply the law, the standard, that it should have applied, and the man was executed. But in that case, as you well know, he was cut off, he wasn't able to be where his troops were. But the standard was so high that they said basically it was almost as if it was strict liability. He was liable because he was a commander and didn't take into account the other factors. And since then I think the pendulum has swung back and now it's right where it should be because you look at all these things. So the Blaskic Appeals Chamber held that command responsibility is not a form of strict liability; that's on paragraph 57. The fact that the superior is in a commanding position does not in and of itself make him liable for the crimes of his subordinates. And I'm not admitting or conceding that any subordinates were committing crimes. According to Celibici -- the Celibici Appeals Chamber the standard is knew or would have known criminal negligence did not again satisfy this standard. Now, third, the Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that he failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish the crimes. When we talk about the punishment aspect, I'm going to refer you back to Mr. Drinic who came -- he had been a Prosecution witness on their list. They questioned him for two days. They didn't bring him in; they brought in somebody else. But Mr. Drinic was able to tell us as a military Prosecutor, and there was another witness as well, and they were able to tell us what the conditions were at the time, because a superior is not required to do the impossible. You notice in my trial brief I indicated that during a period of time there was no witness protection, you could not make a complaint anonymously. The protections that are afforded to the witnesses that we have here do not exist. And of course, the fact that we have these protections and the fact that we use these protections could tell you or should tell you that even during that period of time one would need those protections if he was in a position where he needed to take measures. But again, it's not required to do the impossible. That's not something that needs to be understood. And it also goes to, for instance, when we talk about Nikolic and the separate chain of command which was sort of, in my opinion, rather despairingly set aside by the Prosecutor, much to my regret, but nonetheless we'll discuss that. So -- now, what constitutes necessary and reasonable measures as a matter -- is a matter of evidence and not law. Again, you've got to look at it from case-to-case basis. So I think that the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision gives us those -- that guidance. All right. Well, I apologise again for having to go into the law, but I always think it's kind of good to look at the law because I find it as sort of the compass that will guide us through our factual journey. But before we get to the factual journey, I want to discuss a little bit about this concept of circumstantial evidence because I think we have two sort of separate positions on it. Mr. McCloskey yesterday said that he is very comfortable with circumstantial evidence. Well, perhaps he should be. The Prosecutor. The Defence lawyer, I don't like it, I don't trust it. I am not so willing to rely on it to the extent that the Prosecution is willing to do so in this particular case, and I'll tell you why. Because circumstantial evidence on its face may look very good but it may turn out to be false. The problem with circumstantial evidence is sometimes it looks so good that you don't take the necessary steps to find out whether it's actually reliable. And I'm going to give a little vignette at some point, but first I just want to share with you what I believe is a current event today that would demonstrate beyond any shadow of a doubt - to use Mr. McCloskey's words - that circumstantial evidence can be misleading. Over a thousand young men from America have died in Iraq based on circumstantial evidence that was used as a pretext to go to war in Iraq. Now, I want to stay out of politics, but what I'm trying to say is here you had some very -- key people, credible people like Colin Powell, standing up in front of the United Nations and saying, "We have the evidence," and it was all circumstantial. And based on that they went to war. And now we find out that, hey, we didn't have it. Another example: In the Krstic case, the Prosecution with Mr. Butler, and I'm going to putz upon him a little bit. I think he's not going to fair too well today, in fact. But in any event he stood up in front of the Krstic Trial Chamber and said, you know, if we look at that intercept that says "up there," and we take Erdemovic's testimony which says, "men from Bratunac" and we piece it together what, we come up with is, up there, Bratunac Brigade intercept, Bratunac men, Bratunac Brigade, enough. And they found beyond a reasonable doubt, beyond a reasonable doubt, which is a pretty high standard, based on that. Now, was what intentional? Of course not but it happened. And there lies the problem, it happened. Now, that's why I think we need to be very careful. And in this Tribunal I tried to in my trial brief to set out some guidance. I know we had some evidence, standards on reviewing evidence. I tried to be a little more helpful, and I added a few of my own which I thought were consistent with the law such as: How do you review the evidence of somebody who's gotten a deal? I mean, it's kind of important. What are some of the indicia that you can look at. But what we know from the jurisprudence here is if you're going to piece together a fact based on circumstantial evidence, various pieces of circumstantial evidence, you have to first exclude all other reasonable and possible explanations. All right. That gives me a little more comfort --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is just a flat-out misstatement of the law. You do not have to exclude all other possible interpretations. This would make proving a case absolutely impossible. It's a fundamental misstatement of the law and it cannot stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, you have to understand that these are the understandings and interpretations of Mr. Karnavas to the law. You may not agree with it, but this is their understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my brief, in my trial brief, I set the standard, I cited the law, and if I said "all," I apologise. I withdraw it's not all. It's reasonable and plausible explanations. All right. Now, what do we mean by that? Can we think of an example that might help us? Well, I have one example from this Court that we did. I think it's important to use something live from this case. And first of all, I want to say at the outset that I'm not attacking anybody; that's number one. Number two, and it has to do with Mr. Butler in an exchange with -- in a previous case with respect to Erdemovic where he misspoke. You recall when I brought it out, I told him that I was very sure that he was an honourable man and that was a mistake. So I put that out on the table, right now. But I'm going to show you how I got there. And I'm doing this because I want to show you - and perhaps it's not necessary - but I want to show you why I think it's necessary to go through these machinations in order to be fair, if nothing else. As you may recall, during the Krstic trial there was an exchange between Mr. Harmon, I believe, and Mr. Butler where they asked him about Erdemovic and the men that arrived late. And Mr. Butler said Bratunac Brigade. Of course Mr. Harmon knew that was not correct, Mr. Butler knew that wasn't correct, but in the heat of battle, they got the adrenaline, lack of sleep, who knows. Mr. Harmon does what we call looping. It's one of my favourite techniques. You take that part of the question that you really like and you want to emphasise it, and you make it part of your next question, so you loop it. All right? Which means that he heard it, used it, emphasised it, and Butler picked up on it and used it back. Now, if we just look at that, we can draw some conclusions, circumstantially. They knew about it. Then if I go into other knowledge, other conduct, I might be able to show circumstantially, hey, beyond a reasonable doubt they must have been involved in trying to somehow provide false information. However, as I pointed out, in his report he points out specifically that Erdemovic never says they were from the Bratunac Brigade, all right? So that means I have to take that piece of information and factor it into my analysis. And I have to see whether, with that piece of information, is there another reasonable and plausible explanation, and the answer is of course, there is. He misspoke, and Mr. Harmon probably wasn't paying much attention. That's the alternative, plausible explanation. Now you may ask me: Well, what do you think, Karnavas? Well, the answer to that question would be: It doesn't make a difference what I think because you have to look at the evidence. That's what we need to do, look at the facts, not what we think, because yesterday we heard about four hours of thinking, of postulating. They might have done this, or maybe he did that, I don't know, I can't prove it. Not good enough. And you cannot, cannot, and I underscore that, reach a conclusion based on circumstantial evidence, unless you look at all other reasonable and plausible explanations. And I think that is fair, that's necessary, especially if you're the Prosecutor because you have the Prosecutorial means. What am I getting at? What I'm getting at is you cannot and you should not look away or shy away from evidence, from witnesses that might provide a different explanation. And what do we -- and I'm just going to cover the overall picture of the Prosecution's case and then go into more specifics. But what we see from the Prosecution is in their analysis and which they want you to buy into is that they have this habit when they don't like what they hear, that part of the person's testimony is not reliable at all, and there's not a single Defence witness - I don't think - that they like. At least whenever he says something kind, something good, something positive, something exculpatory, something that would lead you to a reasonable and alternative plausible explanation for Mr. Blagojevic, they don't like that. That part, that witness is not credible. Now, if that same witness has something that can put him right into the mix of things by hook or crook, by stretch, however, oh, we like that part. Oh, yes. So it's almost like we have these witnesses that are bipolar. Whenever they're going to say something positive about Colonel Blagojevic, they're not credible. But if it's something that we be able might to use circumstantially to say that he's in, then obviously they're credible, take it to the bank, rely on it. That's their general theory. What I'm suggesting here, before I go into more of the facts, is that we be very, very careful before we draw these conclusions based on circumstantial evidence. And we try to, we try to, point out alternative plausible explanations in our brief. And I also have the caveat, just because we happen to raise one, but you see it, go for it, sue sponte, ex officio, however you call it. But I think that is only fair. And I started my closing argument, and maybe it's a little bit unusual for this Tribunal, maybe I'm too much of a trial lawyer in front of a jury, but in essence what I was trying to show is that the importance of being fair to the accused. That's what we want to do. We want to be fair to the accused. We have to look at all the evidence, not some of it. And what gets me going a little bit is, for instance, when they quote something in their brief but they omit critical information that might be relevant for you. They take it out of context. I think that's unfair. I think that's denying you the ability to look at that other alternative plausible explanation. And one that comes to mind, for instance, and we may get to it. I have piles of documents as you can see. We won't be able to get to all of them, but there's one, for instance, where they're making a reference to that very special instruction that we talked about, Mladic's instruction, 1994, regarding the separate chains of commands. Now, we've had testimony from all sorts of people. We've gone over that document, and we've had it translated and retranslated. And if you look at their brief, and I can get my hands on it right now, but if we look at their brief and I think it's on paragraph 394 to 399. But if you look at it they quote the one section, they quote the one section out of context. And that's what troubles me, and I mentioned this right now because this is going to be my theme where I hammer and hammer and hammer away at this. Because on 396, paragraph 396 they quote: "Members of the security and intelligence organs must provide their immediate superiors with information, assessment and observations regarding the security units or institutions." Fair enough. But what's missing? What's the part that's missing? "To the extent and in the measure necessary," that's what precedes it. Now, if we did this in front of a jury, I can assure you that they would just all look at the same time. And my question is: Why? Why not quote it as is and say, hey, even though it says this, qualify it. Not a problem. But to omit that part, that critical part, in my book is somewhat misleading. And also, as I have indicated, it doesn't allow you to focus on any other alternative plausible explanations. There are lots more in their brief, but in any event I just wanted to point that one out real quick. And we'll talk a little bit about the separate chain of command, but that's why we have to be extremely careful with circumstantial evidence. Now, let me talk about -- let me get into the thick of things, and I'm first going to talk a little bit in general about this history the way they view it. I already talked about 1992 or 1993 with the stated goals of the RS. As I indicated, it would be fair -- it would be unfair for you, in my opinion, to look at that, especially since we were not permitted nor should we have been permitted to go into what Mr. Izetbegovic was doing, what his aspirations were, how he spent time in prison because he wanted to create an Islamic state during the Tito years and all of that. I don't think that was necessary. But then let's move on further ahead. The Prosecution then mentions directive 7. It was directive 4, they said yesterday they don't know whether he read it or not, whether Mr. Blagojevic read it or not. Then they moved on to directive 7 and directive 7.1. Then they point to some sections, that if you read them in -- if you read them out and you take them out of context, you are left with one particular conclusion. But with respect to Srebrenica, I think you have to look at Krivaja 95, you have to look at the entire document and not just the one section of it, and what was the reasoning and what was the purpose and what did those people at the time think was going on. This is a critical aspect of this case. It's extremely difficult as a Defence to try to focus on the target, because it keeps moving. How do I mean? They say, based on what was happening historically at the time, the Srebrenica enclave was militarised. They were -- in my opinion, they were conducting terror activity, small-scale, but nonetheless sufficient enough to tie down the troops over the there. At the same time, you had the Muslim army getting re-armed from the outside. They already numerically had -- were stronger than the VRS. It was only a matter of time -- and of course we had the intelligence, and we heard from the intelligence officer himself, Mr. Salapura, tell us there was information, and we brought it here, we had this information, there's documents, there's evidence to show that there was this information, and even Mr. Butler himself indicated that as the war was going on at that period of time, it was very clear that at some point the Muslim army was going to attack, and it was going to be able to overpower the VRS. And he indicated that the pre-emptive strike was not against the law, it was okay. So if we stop right there with their analysis, okay, it would seem to me at least that there is no need to argue what happened prior to the attack. What do I mean? By -- if we're talking about the May 25th incident, the Prosecution wants you to think that somehow that day was historic. And why was it historic? For two reasons, because Colonel Blagojevic took over the reins, and two there was the incident. We talked about the incident -- they talked about it yesterday and we heard some testimony. There's no denying it, there's no minimising it. But you want to put it into context. We had the NIOD report. We didn't commission it, neither did the Prosecution. What the NIOD report indicated was that there was a specific reason why that attack took place on that particular day. And the reason it took place was because they were responding to bombings by NATO on Pale and other places. Now, I'm not saying that that was justification but that was the reason, not somehow Colonel Blagojevic arrives in Bratunac and all of a sudden here is his opening salvo to the folks of Srebrenica, I've arrived, incoming. That's nonsense. Number one. Number two, look at who issued the order. The order was issued from the VRS -- from the Drina Corps and it was issued directly. Did the fact that Colonel Blagojevic take the reins of the Bratunac Brigade that day have any -- play any role in this? Absolutely not. At least we have no direct or indirect evidence. Zero. We can speculate. What else does the Prosecution want us to believe? That placing him there was a prelude to what would happen in Srebrenica so they wanted one of their best men in there in advance. Where is the nexus? Where is the connection? It's easy to look back at history and say, hey, now if we look at it this way, they probably did this and that and the other, but you have to be able to link it. You have to have some concrete evidence. You can't just speculate. I have to tell you, at the end of the day I told my colleagues it was like being in the old country and having somebody look at the coffee cup. You know, you turn it over and try to read it. That's what it seemed like yesterday where they are looking into this big -- all of these events and they're able to say this is what happened and this is why. So this attack on Srebrenica first they say it's not a crime. Well, if it's not a crime, then why are we bringing in May 25th and it's not even in the indictment? He's not charged with that, so why are we going there? It's not in -- the attack is legal but nonetheless from there we can make some inferences. As a Defence what are you supposed to do? Well, if I'm told it's not in the indictment, I don't need to defend it. Then I come here and I'm told -- I hear all this. Then I'm beginning to think, well, maybe I should have gone that route because now we're outside the indictment. But in this system we have to stay in, that straightjacket, remember? Now, before I go on to that section let me back up a little bit and stick with Colonel Blagojevic because they're saying somehow, they look at his history and they say, well, he was with the Zvornik Brigade, then from there he went to the Drina Corps. Of course they omitted to say that he went as the Chief of Staff to the Bratunac Brigade. Kind of a, you know, commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Chief of Staff. Then he gets there on May 25th back in the Bratunac Brigade. But let's look at it -- let's look at it for what it is. How long is Colonel Blagojevic with the Zvornik Brigade? Two months. Two months. Who replaces him? A younger officer. What is he doing in the Drina Corps? Do we know? Nobody knows. At least we haven't heard evidence. The assumption that somehow because you move to the Drina Corps and you have a job over there to do, that somehow you are in the sanctum santorum of all the decision makers. But that's what they would have you believe. Because since he's there and he's moved to the Bratunac Brigade, it must have been because he's their main man. He's the homeboy coming back to Bratunac who's going to lead the charge on to Srebrenica. Where is the evidence? There isn't any. It's pure speculation. There's none of that. Not to mention back on May 25th who knows about Srebrenica. Is there any linkage or any connection or any piece of evidence that shows that Colonel Blagojevic at that point in time knows anything about Srebrenica. Now, the other assumption is that since he's from that area obviously they wanted to put him in there because of the campaign. Where's the linkage? How do you get there? He could have easily gone to Milici or someplace else. They just happened to need somebody in the Bratunac Brigade. Can we make the assumption that because he's from that area, he grew up in a village, then he went to the JNA, served outside the area but automatically knows the reason. Can we assume that? Based on what? Based on what? You heard the testimony of Mr. Kovacevic who was the commander, I believe, of the 2nd Company of the 2nd Battalion. And remember he had gone to Zvornik. It's not too far. You've been there. You think when you're driving the car it's pretty close. When he got out on the terrain, he said that he got lost. That's one of the reasons he didn't want to go out there. Same thing with Mico Gavric. He didn't want to go out there because you get lost in the terrain, you don't know the terrain. And what do we hear from one of the witnesses? In Kula, during this critical period - I'm going to talk a little bit about that as well - you had his own men say that Colonel Blagojevic was looking over the maps and trying to figure out what peaks were where and what was the terrain like. He hasn't served there, he doesn't know the terrain. Because he hadn't been there. He had been away. He hadn't served in that area. He hadn't walked that terrain. But to make these assumptions is very dangerous. And you just can't make them out of thin air. And that's what I'm getting at. Because I think if the Prosecution brings a charge, they should have the facts, concrete facts. Now, let me get back to Srebrenica. They say that the attack is not a crime, yet they continue and continue and continue to bring it into the picture. Then yesterday you saw how they went through that -- they went through his order of July 5th, 1995. Now, what they don't tell you is everybody else that looked at it said that this was a perfectly fine order. Mr. -- General Keserovic who came here, testified how with respect to the prisoners, and I invite your close scrutiny and attention to his testimony, he talked about -- he compared the Drina Corps order with respect to how the prisoners should be handled versus what was in Colonel Blagojevic's order. And he said: This is the correct way, versus General Zivanovic's which more or less left it up to the security organ. Had made no provisions whatsoever for logistics.. Then they went and said: Well, look at this order. A defence. It's important. They play an important part. Well, let's stop here and take a deep breath. The interpreters may want that as well. What does that tell us? Well, they were there the whole time. It wasn't like they got there and they're playing defence. You know? I mean, I can understand the Prosecution's position the defence is important. We saw that during the European football cup, you know, the team with the best defence, the Greeks. They won the cup. They didn't have the talent, but it was the defence that got them winning. So I understand that defence is important. But you also have to understand, and it wasn't quite as highlighted as I would have liked, but they were there the entire time. They played no role. But the attack was never a crime. But now at some point on the 9th we know that the game plan changes. All right? And now orders are from the top that they're going to take over Srebrenica. So now we might be a little concerned. But still, there is no, as far as I know, in the indictment nothing that says that the taking over of the enclave was a crime. Mind you, mind you, we had Karremans himself and the others all said that this was a militarised enclave. It was demilitarised. So everyone had their own concerns, but it wasn't a crime. Of course they had to consider, those who made the decision, that by taking over Srebrenica you would be stuck with those civilians there. I think the U.S. is finding that out now in Baghdad.
