They didn't realise it at the time. Easy to go in, hard to maintain. They should have thought of that. And I agree with the Prosecution there that at that point some thought should have been put into. But again, where is the connection? How is it -- where is Colonel Blagojevic in the Bratunac Brigade in this picture? Is he consulted? Is he involved? They say, well, he took this walk down to Srebrenica and probably did or did not meet with General Mladic. Let's look at the evidence. The evidence is that he's in Pribicevac, that area, Kula, from the 6th to the 11th. In comes General Krstic who is the Chief of Staff at the time of the Drina Corps. Now, what does he do? Here's how to handle your main man. You kick him out of the forward command post, take over, and then you send him a hundred yards or so into a ditch and then say, okay, make your forward command post over there and not consult with him anymore because that's the evidence of -- the Prosecution would have us believe it's all nonsense. Where is the proof that it isn't -- that it is? Where? What is their evidence? Well, they're all loyalists of Colonel Blagojevic, so they all must be untruthful. Based on what? Show me one document, one document, point to one witness that said that there was a close connection between Colonel Blagojevic and General Krstic, the relationship, where was it? It's not there. But we have testimony that Colonel Blagojevic was in essence kicked out of the forward command post as a lieutenant colonel or colonel at the time and told to go in a ditch and he's sitting over there. He has a make-shift forward command post and he's not consulted. Is that how you treat your main man, the person that's going to lead all of this and do all of this? Hardly. When you compare how Pandurevic was treated and the role that he played and the troops that he had and the involvement that he played, then you begin to see night and day difference. Then they bring in P135. Who can forget P135? I can't? It was one of the most memorable experiences in court for me. You know. After the first day you asked me whether I was trying to show that he was a liar. I said no -- I didn't answer the question if you go back. Those are his words, not mine. Second day he asked for protection from you because he was afraid of the lawyer, me. Then somehow we find out that he was complaining that during the proofing session the Prosecution was shutting the drawer and yelling at him. He was all over the place like a little bumblebee. I have to tell you, it was like shadow boxing with the guy because he couldn't keep an answer straight to save his life. Then what do we have at the end? The Prosecutor says the man was not -- was embellishing. So how credible is this guy? I suggest he's not. Do you have any concrete evidence. I'm not saying he's a bad person. But probably, you know, a lot of that is in his mind. Maybe he wanted to be a hero, I don't know. But if you look at the facts and you look at what he was saying, it just doesn't make sense. But then you also have to -- if you're going to take that and you are going to build on it and embrace it like the Prosecution does, because they like it. They like what they hear, and that's what I said earlier. Whenever they hear something that's for them, they embrace it. Never mind that it's not credible. If you're going to do that, ask yourselves is there anything else that backs up that witness P135 was credible? But now he's the protege. Where did that come out of? That's the first time I heard it yesterday, protege. Heaven help us from those sorts of folks. So what else do we know about that period of time? We know that there was no shelling, like the Prosecution says, of Srebrenica. If you look at the documents - and I have it here buried someplace - they would have you believe at one point that from Pribicevac you can look down and see Srebrenica and shell it. Butler makes reference to it, it's in their final brief, and guess what, and I thought I would bring this out because I think it's a little circumstantial evidence of my own. When we were putting that little trip sightseeing trip to visit the various sites, interesting enough what was missing from the Prosecution's list, the first list, was Pribicevac. Imagine to have this entire case --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, going into the details and the planning of that trip and offering these inferences and getting into misstatements of what the Prosecution feels you can see from there is way out of line, and I apologise for interrupting but this is going into outer space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On this part I agree with Mr. Peter McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think you have a point in your argument but don't make it too argumentative. Just present your view and your understandings on certain evidence and issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I wasn't aware that I was being argumentative, but if you say I am then I must be. But just to touch up on that last point with Pribicevac, and I don't want to beat the point to death, but in their brief on paragraph 40 it says, and I quote: "Drina Corps units were headquartered at the village of Pribicevac, which is looked -- which is located in the hills overlooking the town of Srebrenica." And then you have to look at the footnotes. And as you all know I relish footnotes because I like to go to them and check them out and lo and behold most of the time you get disappointed. But first of all, he Drina Corps were not headquartered in the village of Pribicevac; that's first of all. They were headquartered in Vlasenica. They had an IKM, a forward command post, but they certainly didn't have headquarters there. Then if you look at -- and then they say there is a photo, Exhibit 12, overlooking Srebrenica town with the playground. But is that from Pribicevac? I don't know. We weren't able to find that. I'm sure it's there someplace, but you were up in Pribicevac and you can't see the town. Then you can see in footnote 81 it says: "Pribicevac is condition Mount Olovine overlooking the town of Srebrenica," and they point to transcript page 4350. So if you go to 4350 and you look at it, and it's Mr. Butler's testimony, I dare say you will be disappointed. There won't anything about it, and you won't be able to see it. And again, I point this out as a vignette so I can cover the point that, one, you cannot see anything from Pribicevac, and also the point that somehow some of these little things get snuck in inadvertently, I'm sure, but nonetheless they shouldn't be in there. But they want to make the case that there they were shelling. Where is there evidence that the Bratunac Brigade did any shelling of Srebrenica town? And mind you, as I understand, you were all able to go to Srebrenica. Did you see anything of the shells that they are talking about? There is no evidence. There's none that I have been able to see. Now, there is incidentally some -- they do reference -- while I'm at -- on the point, they do reference a 92 bis witness that came in, Mr. Kingori. He testified in the Krstic trial and his testimony came in from the Krstic trial. He was a UN military observer. Interesting. Interesting because when I went to look him up, guess what he says. He's emphatic in the Krstic trial testifying in front of the Honourable Members of that Tribunal [sic] that at the time -- that at this particular time Srebrenica was completely demilitarised because it had been declared an enclave. Now, why do I mention that? Just as an aside, because here if he says contrary to all evidence -- even the Prosecution admits that Srebrenica was militarised, he's there at the time, he's walking around, he's seeing what's going on, and he's saying under oath to the Judges that Srebrenica was demilitarised, didn't have any weapons because they had given up all their weapons. I think you can take that and draw all sorts of conclusions such as maybe he has a creative imagination, maybe his testimony is not trustworthy. Well, those are the kind of conclusions that I draw because I don't think that you can be a UN military observer in Srebrenica and say that it was demilitarised when we have Karremans who was there who said it was getting militarised. Mind you, his own people were held at gunpoint and held hostage for 30 days by the Bandera Triangle. So anyway, I just point that out. Your Honours, I don't know how am I doing on the time? I can keep going or it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you finish that section?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think I finished the section, and I might be speaking a little faster than I should. I can keep going. I mean, it's just -- but it might be a good opportunity to sort of take a breather, but it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems that we have to stop every hour and maybe we'll take the break right now and we'll resume at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, just for your information we'll sit until 1.30, and that will be three and a half hours in the morning session. And in the afternoon session you still one hour to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. It won't be enough, Your Honour. It won't be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just getting warmed up. Okay. Now, I want to get to the 11th and the 12th, the meetings at Hotel Fontana and what have you. But first I really want to touch a little bit on this All People's Defence, that at one point I believe, Mr. President, you said I was obsessed with. And I wasn't. But I wanted to make a point, and I think it's an important point, and I want to explain why. Because we have to understand the events in context. One of the reasons brought it out was - and if you go back to Mr. Butler's testimony, Mr. Butler comes from the United States, it's a different system, military system, he came and he reviewed the regulations, and of course he relied a lot of his information and based a lot of his analysis by reading the regulations and also by speaking to some of the witnesses. He indicated that he did not consult with any local experts, local military experts. By that I mean that were, you know, non-Serb or non-Muslim. They could have gone to Croatia, Slovenia, Macedonia, they could have gone elsewhere to look for someone that might be able to give him some of that local knowledge that I believe was necessary. He didn't do that. And if you recall there's an exchange where I ask him about the All People's Defence. He said he was familiar with it, but he paid no real mind to it. He really didn't think it was that necessary. Now, the reason I kept asking all the witnesses about All People's Defence wasn't because I needed to know about it, or -- and I figured early on that you understood what the concept was. So it wasn't as if I was trying to beat a dead horse as the saying goes, but rather what I wanted to show was this concept is so prevalent, so all-knowing for those people that lived in that part of the world. That to begin to understand society as it functions and how the military works in conjunction with civil organs, you cannot even begin unless you know the military doctrine as it existed. Because Mr. Butler, his position was, well, the VRS is an extension of the JNA, save for a few modifications. What he left out was the core military doctrine. And the core military doctrine -- in fact, the entire nation had been indoctrinated, if you will, in that. Everyone understood and knew that they had a vital and important role to play, whether they were a man or a woman. You served your military duty, you would be on the reserve. If you were a woman, you would have a particular task. But everybody understood -- and you even had classes. Remember, we had the one gentleman who said he was a teacher and he said that he taught. I asked him: Was that one class? He says, no, no, that was every grade. The whole purpose of the All People's Defence was if there was an invasion of Yugoslavia, because the JNA was never an army developed to attack outside but rather to defend the motherland. And the way they worked it was you would have the professional army but then you would have the Territorial Defences that would be working in conjunction. And they had drills. And because of this concept, this war was rather unique because it was easy for all sides, all factions to take their Territorial Defences and turn them and mobilise them into armies. The Croats did it, the Muslims did it, the Serbs did it. Also what's important about the All People's Defence is this mobilisation process and the workings with the Ministry of Defence. Now, why was that important for the Defence because if you look at it from the abstract and circumstantial evidence -- and here's again where I part company with Mr. McCloskey. If we just look at the events and you say, okay, there's the meetings at Hotel Fontana on the 11th. On the 12th you have one meeting. All of a sudden buses and trucks arrive, therefore, therefore, what can we conclude? Quite easy, that there was a plan well in advance to mobilise, to get all these vehicles, to get all that fuel --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise. But I have repeatedly stated in this trial that that is not the theory of our case. And I think I stated in my closing argument that they got this together suddenly and that I think the All People's Defence helped them be able to get those buses together. And if time is going to be an issue, perhaps that will save us some time, but I don't know how many times I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. All right. Now, if I can point out -- you know, see, I love these mea culpas, but they are not enough, they are not sufficient, because when we go to paragraph 100 of their brief -- there's a reason why I'm saying these things because I'm a little paranoid. I look at their brief -- paragraph 100: "The fact that the operation appeared well planned underscores the coordination that had to have occurred and commanded levels of the various units involved as well as the primacy given to the forcible transfer operation in light of the diversion of resources involved at a time when the VRS was seeking to redirect its assets to the Zepa front." Now, we have an admission here but I have this to deal with. As I said, the target is moving. And so which one is it? And what I'm trying to say is also -- and I can appreciate Mr. McCloskey and I welcome -- he can -- if he has any more concessions, you know, now's the time. But what I'm trying to use this also as a vehicle of circumstantial evidence. Because if you're looking at it from the outside not knowing of this All People's Defence, you say, my God, how can they all get there. Even Mr. Karremans thought, he thought that there was some kind of plan between the Serbs and the Muslims, you know, the government in Sarajevo, and that's how they were able to mobilise. Again, I'm trying to show the dangers of circumstantial evidence. But also this mobilisation process, they were -- everybody was supposed to comply with it, and we had the one witness, the one soldier from the Bratunac Brigade whose bus was mobilised. And he went to the local authorities. He didn't like it but decided that he was going to drive his bus anyway because he didn't want somebody else driving it because they were going to take it. There was fuel for it, and the gentleman did go to Potocari. And then -- and I say this with some degree of discomfort that the Prosecution uses that as a vehicle to suggest that somehow this individual or others that were there helping out some friends knew of this genocidal plan, that's why they wanted to get them out. It's in the brief, Your Honour. It's in the brief. I felt the same way. That's why I said, it's of some discomfort. It appears that no good deed goes unpunished. But what was in those people's minds, they saw that the person was being separated, they wanted to help him out, and it appears that even a good Samaritan now, we turn it around and say, ah. He knew about it, he must have known about it, and he was a member of the Bratunac Brigade. Therefore, his commander for sure would know about it, thus the kind of circumstantial evidence that they're dealing with. Also I wanted to bring this mobilisation process into play in the All People's Defence because of the use of the fuel. I'm going to touch upon this a little bit even though I'm going to get ahead of myself. When I had Mr. Butler on the stand there was some hypotheticals. You can go through them, Your Honours, it's in the testimony, but I'm talking about the functional relationship, Drina Corps, Bratunac Brigade, rear services. Again, circumstantial evidence. This is how dangerous, insidious it is. Circumstantial evidence and not the witnesses. They see the logbook that says all this fuel from the Bratunac Brigade was consumed. Butler from there extracts this conclusion that because the fuel was such a large amount it would have been outside the functional relationship in a sense because here the Drina Corps is siphoning up all of the fuel of the Bratunac Brigade, and therefore, from there we can extract another conclusion and that is that Major Trisic would have most definitely informed his commander, Colonel Blagojevic. All from that. Now, a couple of points. First, Major Trisic had been interviewed by the OTP. They could have brought him on if they wanted to advance those theories; they did not. Can we draw any conclusions? Well, I can tell you that I can draw plenty of them, but I will leave that up to you why they didn't call him to at least explain in his own words what those documents meant. We brought him. Secondly, we had Mr. Trisic explain that this is an accounting procedure, that the fuel belongs to the Drina Corps, not to the Bratunac Brigade. But somebody has to take accounting for it. But then -- so therefore you cannot make any conclusions as somehow because of this accounting procedure Colonel Blagojevic would have been notified. Again, we brought that information to you, another plausible, reasonable explanation. And again, ask yourselves: Why wasn't he brought in by the Prosecution? All right. Let's don't dwell on it. But then he explains away all of that. But also if we go back to the meetings in the Hotel Fontana we see that at some point General Mladic says: We'll provide the buses, you're going to have to provide the fuel. All right. Now, let's park a little bit over there; let's pause. Now, the Prosecution's case began with them bringing in a slough of Dutch folks of DutchBat, and what was their theory? Remember Major Boering? In fact, I can remember it like yesterday. There was even an admonition from the trial bench, and rightly so, because perhaps we were a little bit too exuberant with the gentleman when he was being cross-examined. But through Major Boering they were trying to establish that it was the VRS, it was General Mladic, who had initiated the meeting. Why is that important? Yes, Mr. President, because there is a whole exchange between me and Major Boering, and the implication was that somehow the Prosecution at that point in time - the theory was - that it was the VRS, General Mladic, who initiated the meeting and was also the one who initiated the concept of the forcible transfer. And I asked him some questions about Karremans. Of course Karremans we know was in Spain. We brought him; the Prosecution could have, but we brought him. And he was able to fill in some gaps for us. He told us that the UN contacted him and told him to contact the VRS to begin to arrange for the evacuation process of the people that are gathered in Potocari. And you're going to see a reference in the brief of the Prosecution, the final brief, where again there is a -- there is an error. And the error is that they point to one section of the brief where -- of the transcript of Colonel Karremans where he is going through his mental process and then you'll see -- I ask pointedly right after that concretely: What happened at the Hotel Fontana? You see the film. And there we see that Karremans comes clean and tells us that he had been ordered to make arrangements. We also know through Colonel Karremans and through the NIOD report that the UN had been talking about this, the local government had been talking about this, and so this was -- this wasn't something that was initiated by General Mladic. I think that's relevant. I think the fact that the Prosecution makes a big issue of the trucks being mobilised and somehow the Bratunac Brigade must have known all about it. Well, think about it. Let's stop -- let's park again over here and stop. We're in Hotel Fontana, we're the fly on the wall, we're watching and we're seeing what's going on. In fact, we're shadowing, we're shadowing, General Mladic. If you were there on those particular days what you would have heard is General Mladic -- okay, he was yelling at Karremans. Karremans was not being very responsive, let's face it. We saw him on the video. He was scared. All right. But it was very clear that Karremans had approached him for the evacuation. There is this exchange. It's clear afterwards - and I believe it's on the 12th and I'll be corrected if I'm wrong - that General Mladic for the first time says, "We're going to screen the military aged men to look for war criminals." All right. And then we have -- if we pan over to Potocari and we see General Mladic, we see him addressing the folks. Everybody that hears General Mladic says: You can go wherever you want to go, nothing will happen to you, we're going to separate the men. What am I driving at? Why would anybody think differently? Can we make that assumption that everybody knew that General Mladic was lying to all these people? That General Mladic had this genocidal intent? That he had all these other plans? From where can we derive? How can we extract that and say Colonel Blagojevic must have known, because the meeting happened in Bratunac. What is the knowledge of his men, what their hear? Why would they question what they hear? Think about it. And I throw that out because now it is an important factor. So before we start jumping to conclusions that all those men knew that the separation meant killings and the separation meant genocide, we have to pause and ask ourselves what did those men know at that particular time based on what information when they heard their own general, the head of the army saying: You will go wherever you want to go, we're just going to screen these people. And we'll talk about the other stuff that happens later on. The Prosecution has maintained from day one, and it's in the indictment, that straightjacket, that the plan to execute everybody was on the night of the 11th or 12th. It's in the indictment, black and white, there. We have it; we can't get away from it. Yesterday it was, well, okay, maybe it was the 12th or the 13th. If not the 12th or the 13th, the 13th for sure. But which one is it? Don't I have to know which one is it if I'm going to defend?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a misstatement of my argument --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is a direct misstatement of my argument, Your Honour, and it's too crucial a point to let that stand. I think you heard the argument. I told you when I thought the plan was held and I supplied you the evidence regarding it. That is a misstatement and it is too crucial for me to be quiet on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, you can read the transcript. There's not need -- and he can get on rebuttal and he can yell all he wants. But that's what he said yesterday. But in any event, we've got the transcript and I'll move on. If you read his final brief he says, well, the moment that General Mladic said that the men are going to be separated, everybody knew at that point that it was genocide time. That's what they argue now. So first there's this meeting, then all of a sudden when he says, "We're going to separate." Which one is it? Stick with your story and let's go with it, but it can't be changing back and forth. And it's changing because they have no evidence, Your Honours. They have no evidence. Yes, Colonel Blagojevic was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade; that doesn't mean that it was involved in anything. Name me one witness, one single witness, who saw Colonel Blagojevic in the meeting. What do they say? Well, we've got Momir Nikolic. All right. Let's talk about Momir Nikolic. Where can I start? I need a day just an Momir Nikolic. But let me just say: What is it Momir Nikolic tells us? He says on the morning of the 12th I'm standing in front of the Hotel Fontana and that's when I here from Popovic and Kosoric that there's going to be this plan to kill everybody, and they're asking me where we could find places to do the killings. All right. Let's freeze the frame right there. Now, if you recall and you go back, and I invite your close scrutiny and attention to that rather contentious cross-examination. On that particular point I was trying -- I asked him a question. Did he see himself on the video. He wouldn't answer. And then, Mr. President, he asked you him the question, and he answered and he said yes. Do you remember I asked him if he could let us peek into the mind of somebody who's trying to create a story because he admitted that he had lied - that's the word that he used - to the Prosecution. And he told us that he wanted to make a deal with the Prosecutor. Everything he kept giving them, they already had. So he needed to give them something they didn't have. Now, what did he have in his possession? All the disclosure material, from indictment to every single document, including the videos. So he looks at the video and then he can say, well, I'm in front of the Hotel Fontana, 11th and 12th. Well, how do you know? Well, look at my video. And that's how he begins to concoct his story. Now I've got to tell you, I'm a little troubled by Momir Nikolic, and I'm a little troubled about the way it was handled because he's the only witness that was debriefed, at least that I know of, important witness who was cooperating where they didn't tape-record all those sessions. Now, I've got to tell you, I'm a little suspicious. But I know for sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, that's not true. Obrenovic was dealt with the exact same way. And his suspicions about some speculated evil of the Prosecution, have we not had enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You're out of your line at this point. Please concentrate on your theory of the interpretation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to concentrate, Your Honour. Because somehow we have Momir Nikolic who gives them all this information based on the information that he has from the Prosecution. Then what happens, the Prosecution doesn't check it and we have the one incident with Mile Petrovic where somebody is accused of killing six people. Now that made international news. That was on the front page of The Herald Tribune around the world saying "first Serbian officer to admit," and so on and so forth, and there's this grisly description of how he talks about Mile Petrovic killing somebody. They didn't bother to go check it out. He was with Mirko Jankovic, supposedly; that wasn't checked out. Statements with the Bratunac police department; those weren't checked out. They did nothing to check out that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He doesn't know what the Prosecution did fully. He had questions on it. What on God's green earth is the purpose of this? How is he defending his client? He's not. He's defending his own ego. And it's repulsive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, don't do some speculative argument at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if we could point out to one piece of evidence where they talk to Mile Petrovic or something because we had those gentlemen here. What I'm trying to suggest, Your Honour, is every time that there is a piece of evidence that is helpful to their case they cling on to it, no matter what. They don't check it. Because they are not interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Making an attack or argument with the Prosecution is not the purpose of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you have a point, you know, just tell us what's your understanding of the theories of the case. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The point that I'm trying to make is there are other reasonable and plausible explanations that the Prosecution was never interested in, and yesterday we didn't hear one single one of them. And I have to wonder. I have to wonder why all of the Defence witnesses somehow are not credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can get up and defend our honour all day long, and I will. But this is not defending his client; it's a constant attack on the Prosecution. It's a theory best left for American politics and not in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I believe that you have to cool down, although you've said you haven't warmed up yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Very well. Let's talk about the yellow bridge where it was Mr. Waespi that called our Serbian witness that he was engaged in convoy terror. I think we can remember how the gentleman reacted to that. The Prosecution's theory is that somehow Colonel Blagojevic was involved in that as well, that as soon as he took over the Bratunac Brigade that he was engaged in this convoy terror or a procedure like that. Again, the Prosecution fails to look at any other plausible and reasonable explanations such as, for instance, the evidence that shows that this was a Main Staff operation, that the witnesses that came -- okay, granted, they were Defence witnesses. So I guess we need to be suspect of that. But what did they say? If there was a problem at the checkpoint they contacted either the Drina Corps or the Main Staff, not Colonel Blagojevic. That's on the record. Do we hear that from them? No. Why? Another plausible and reasonable explanation. What was the purpose of the gentleman who came here and was attacked, in my opinion, as far as trying to starve out the people in Srebrenica, what was his answers? His answer was, look, I look at the manifest. If there's something in the truck that's not on the manifest, I have orders not to let it go. That's all. But somehow they try to make this out to be that the Bratunac Brigade and that Colonel Blagojevic specifically was involved in this. There's no evidence of that. I talked a little bit about the meetings. We don't have a single meeting where Colonel Blagojevic attends. The Prosecution would have you believe, if you read between the lines, that Momir Nikolic was there on behalf of Colonel Blagojevic and that he was reporting to him and that -- and yesterday we heard this absurd - and that's the only word I can come up with - that this absurd theory that since Drago Nikolic and Obrenovic had this close relationship that it must have existed between Momir Nikolic and Colonel Blagojevic because they shared the same positions. But what did we hear when we had Mr. Nikolic on the stand, Momir? He said from the 6th to the 11th he had no contact with his commander. Do you remember that? How many times did I ask that? I said 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th. I kept repeating it over and over and over again. I wanted to drum it home to everybody. Because here is the guy who is the head of intelligence and security. The Prosecutor would have you believe that as of the 12th this guy who doesn't report to his commander all of a sudden is reporting. All of a sudden he's operating consistent with the chain of command. And I questioned him: Wasn't this the most important campaign of the Bratunac Brigade? After all Momir Nikolic had been the commander of the Territorial Defence before the Bratunac Brigade was established. And commanders kept coming and going, but there was Momir Nikolic with his Ray Bans, smoking his Marlboros, dressed to the nines, and he was there. He knew exactly what was going on. Where was he during those critical days? Nowhere to be found. Was there an answer from the Prosecution or from Momir Nikolic explaining his activities? Zero. Is that another plausible and reasonable explanation that we can draw from, that piece of evidence? Yes. That tells us that he here's a guy who does whatever he wants. He's self-managing. Do you remember the very last question, Mr. President? You asked him about his relationship. And then it was as if he was speaking in a normal tone, and then all of a sudden there was a switch as if he was some place else; you had touched a nerve. And he talked about how he had to drive I don't know how many kilometres away to give orders to the military police because the military police would not respond to Colonel Blagojevic. Do you remember that? And from that little exchange we saw a lot. We saw somebody who had absolutely no respect for Colonel Blagojevic, for his own commander. And what do we see? We see that throughout this period that he is with Popovic and he's with Beara. Now let me go back to the 11th -- the morning of the 12th. The Prosecution would have us believe that Nikolic is an honest witness on that event. Never mind they wanted to bring in Witness 130 who was going to say that Nikolic had committed perjury. But think about it. If he told Popovic where to take those bodies and he's telling him, and if he's so close with Beara why does Beara on the morning of the 14th need to try to locate the brick factory? Why is Beara talking to Deronjic on the night of the 13th? He's got Nikolic, if this is occurring. Nikolic can show him around. Why does Nikolic have to go up to General Mladic supposedly to report in Konjevic Polje - and there's absolutely no evidence to that - but he said, "I went to give a reporting and I asked the general what will happen to the men." And he says -- he did one of these. Well, if you already know why would you even go up to Mladic, not to mention everybody ran away from Mladic. This is the only witness that ran toward him. We heard what Mladic would do to soldiers, usually slap them. So -- but I bring back if this really happened on the 12th, why would Beara need to talk to Deronjic? Now, interestingly enough, Deronjic, the capo de capo [phoen] of Bratunac, Mr. SDS. This guy was number one by everybody's standard. Everybody. There wasn't a single witness that we brought in that didn't say that he was the number one, and Deronjic even admitted it himself. Now, yesterday -- interestingly enough, just as an aside, the Prosecution's office has given him effectively what I call immunity because the deal he made with the Prosecution was: Whatever you tell us we won't use against you with Srebrenica. So of course then they came out and said we don't have any evidence. I mention this, Your Honour, because yesterday, yesterday for the first time we heard a disassociation of the Office of the Prosecution from Mr. Deronjic. Go back to the transcript, listen to what the Prosecutor said. He basically said, hey, this guy cannot be trusted, cannot be believed. Now ask yourselves why. Going back to my earlier remarks at the beginning of my closing. Deronjic, I had him on the stand for four days, and I have to say that it was rather tense. I'm sure it wasn't a pleasant experience for Mr. Deronjic. For me it was much more pleasant than for him. But it was extremely unpleasant. At times you could see he was visibly shaken because I was putting him, to use Mr. McCloskey's terms, in the vortex of the killings and I was placing blame on him because he was the commissioner of Srebrenica and was responsible for all the civilians. So where am I getting with all of this. We have two things. There's so much, Your Honour. There's so much to cover. Where am I getting with all this? Two points. First of all, Deronjic comes in and says: I don't recall Nikolic being there at that meeting, and then he told us why. I don't want to go into that, but we all know. Now we're beginning to see that maybe Nikolic is not a trustworthy witness. But secondly there was this wonderful question by Judge Vassylenko, and I want to thank you, Judge Vassylenko, because you asked him. And remember what he said. I have been -- for the last four or five years I have been researching this case, investigating it, because he's trying to find out all the facts so he can cover his own back, so he can come up with his own alibis. He can figure out who to massage in order to make sure that he's not in the loop. And what does he say? That all this time, all this time, I haven't heard one single word about Blagojevic. He wasn't at any meetings. He was a man of no importance. He had nothing to do with the SDS. He didn't hear anything. Now, that's a bad fact for the Prosecution. So now we have to say that Deronjic cannot be credible because of that. How can you say he's credible about all these other things but here he's not credible. I mention that, Your Honours, because I think it's important to understand. And what did Deronjic say? They're having this meeting -- he has this meeting on the night of the 13th. He's concerned -- let me back up a little bit, because it is on the afternoon of the 13th, as I recall, that he has a meeting with Borovcanin who is the head of the MUP unit. Borovcanin has come to complain because he's heard that Mladic is leaving town. He's going to Zepa and that the prisoners are going to be the MUP's responsibility, and they don't want that because they have other things to do, they don't have the resources, whatever the case may be. There's no mention about any killings or anything. So he goes and he has this meeting with Deronjic. Deronjic at some point contacts Karadzic and says, hey, what's going on? The whole town of Bratunac is full of these people. Whose are they? What's going to happen to them? And there's that little cryptic message from President Karadzic. Next you know here comes Beara, whiskey bottle in one hand, and he's ready to talk to Deronjic about where to take these prisoners because he's got a job to do. Did we hear any evidence at any time of anybody saying, let's get in Colonel Blagojevic? You remember there was that talk about the safety of the town. Did anybody say: Hey, we should contact Blagojevic. Did anybody? Is there any meeting? Is there any mention? I'm not talking about the mentioning of Colonel Blagojevic in intercepts. But at this critical point -- and then if you want to really believe Nikolic, and I must tell you that I don't see a shred of credibility with that man. He says: I was there, we had all these meetings, it was terrible, then I went and had this private conversation with my commander because I wanted to inform him, it's around midnight. What did you do after that. He said he told his commander: I don't know how we're going to get through the night. Remember? Imagine. A town full of prisoners and you don't know how you're going to go through the night. So what did you do after that, Mr. Nikolic? I went home. Then what did you do? I went to bed. Okay. Does that sound logical? Maybe in Momir Nikolic's world. It certainly doesn't sound logical in anybody else's world. And then the Prosecution wants you to believe that everything is working out according to the chain of command with respect to Momir Nikolic, and every time he says that he has a meeting with Colonel Blagojevic is what I call the four eyes, four ears. There's nothing else to support it, nothing to substantiate it. I'm getting a little excited, Your Honour. It's very difficult not to when I'm speaking about Momir Nikolic. Momir Nikolic tells us that he was the coordinator. What does the Prosecutor do in their brief? They say, well, you know, we brought some Dutch witnesses, and they even say that he was coordinating. I want to bring you back to that one little vignette where we had I believe it was Van Duijn. Tall good-looking young man. And he said that he was able to see what -- he saw Momir Nikolic from afar and from these hand motions you could tell that Momir Nikolic was in command. And I pointed out to him because I had his record that he had been to Greece where we talk with our hands. And I asked him, well, then when you go to Greece you don't need to know the language because you can watch people's hands and figure out what they are saying. And there was an objection at that point. But the point I wanted to drive is this: He walks around, strutting around like a peacock. Dressed good. So maybe he gives off this aura that he has some importance. But what does he say? He says that Colonel Jankovic of the Main Staff, who it would appear is now subordinated to the Drina Corps, has made him the coordinator. Then we have our own witness who comes there and says, yes, I was tasked to make an accounting of all the people that were getting on the buses, I was working with Colonel Jankovic. Now, let's stop here. Here's a colonel. The colonel is tasking a captain, not even first class, reservist, to coordinate all these officers that are above him in rank. And the colonel himself is doing manual labour in Potocari. Now, what's wrong with that picture? It just doesn't fly. What's more, I'm a little troubled. We weren't able to get Mr. Jankovic here, but why wasn't -- why didn't the Prosecution contact Salapura, to bring him here, to explain to us -- we brought Salapura here and he told us that Jankovic was there probably as a liaison officer, he's not a commander, so he cannot give orders. You remember yesterday? Commanders -- remember that whole speech of Beara being an empty vessel? I love that. Empty vessel, Beara. Well, if we take that, Jankovic was certainly much smaller an empty vessel and could not give any orders, and there's absolutely nothing, nothing, nothing that says that Momir Nikolic was coordinating. But we did bring some witnesses here. What did they say? Well, they said that he's walking around. We know on the 13th he's driving a blue car - apparently he has a preference for blue cars - and he picks up a couple of his friends and he drives to Potocari and he walks around. This guy was so narcissistic that if he had been named the coordinator of all these people do you think that he would not tell his friends he's such an important guy. He's a want to be who never was and never will be. He wants to be big, he never was, and he never will be. He wants to get in front of the cameras; that's Momir Nikolic. But we also know on the 14th he goes to the UN trying to collect rent from them, again in that blue car; that he denied. Is there anybody that really said that he was coordinating? The Prosecution said, well, Major Trisic said that he was coordinating. He's walking around and he might be giving some directions to the Bratunac Brigade military police. Is that coordinating all those units? Did he coordinate with Major Trisic who was there to give water and bread? No. Name me one officer that they brought here that said he was the coordinator, not one single one. Yet they would want you to believe -- and he wants them to believe, that's the sad part about this, you see. They want to believe him because they have to believe him because the more important Nikolic is, you see, the more involved Colonel Blagojevic is. That's the key. So if Nikolic is out there coordinating, that means he's there probably with the blessings of his commander and somehow things are working. But we see at no time, at no place does he ever report to anyone. Now, let's talk a little bit about the military police. Again, I apologise to the interpreters. I'm switching topics, but there's so much to cover, so much. I talked a little bit about the yellow bridge, I'll move on. On the morning of the 12th, apparently some of the military police are ordered or tasked, whatever you want to call it, by Momir Nikolic to go into Potocari. We brought those witnesses here. We brought them because we thought it was important. And what did they say? They said, well, we were ordered to go there and we were ordered to stand next to the DutchBat to protect the population. Now, the Prosecution would have you believe that every single one of those folks is not telling the truth. Why -- except with one person, because they did not see any separations. Well, can we apply that same standard, Your Honours, to Mr. Karremans? Karremans was on the stand. Why would he say that he walked around for that two-day period and didn't see separations? He didn't notice the white house. Could it be that there were so many people, there was so much activity, there's all this stuff going on that it's possible that he's just not paying attention. We're not saying it didn't happen, it happened. But why would Karremans say he didn't see it, he didn't see abuses. Think about that. Is it possible that they were just there because they were ordered from Momir Nikolic, and what can you infer from that? They're sitting there and they hear General Mladic say: Nothing will happen to you. It's on the video. You can go wherever you want to go. We can disagree and say, well, they really didn't have a choice. That's a different issue. The point is they're listening to the highest military officer. Why would they have any reason to believe something would happen to them? Mile Janic, the gentleman that came, he said I was tasked to go and report to Colonel Jankovic, and I was then seconded or subordinated to him, and I took an accounting. He was quite specific and if you look at their brief what they cite and if you look at the record, you'll see that there is perhaps -- there is a discrepancy. I asked him specifically whether he counted the men, the answer was yes. I asked him whether he counted them separately, the answer was no. He was just lumping them all in. There was no one taking a separate accounting. He was told to count, he tried to count them initially proper and then he decided it was too much, and so it was about 50 or 60 per bus. Then in the afternoon of the 12th he said the men became restless because of the white house, and so at that point Colonel Jankovic made the decision to send about 10 or so buses. And I don't think there's much disagreement here. We say around 500 or slightly more; they say 750, somewhere in that neighbourhood. But that's when they're sent over there. He says that he sees the folks at the white house. He has no reason to believe that anything was going to happen to them. He guards them at night, I believe. And then the next morning he goes back, he does his duty. Now, I want to focus a little bit on the night of the 13th going into the 14th. A small piece of evidence but I think it speaks volumes. According to Mile Janic, Colonel Jankovic is there for those two days. We even have Franken approaching him with the list. He says, yes, I know, we've got about 6.000 people. I think that tells us that Colonel Jankovic has nothing to fear. Because he doesn't think anything is going to happen. He's not trying to hide the number of people that were captured. He's just making that statement. But what does he do 30 minutes into the 14th. We have the exhibit, I don't have the number. But he writes a note to the intelligence of the Drina Corps and that's how we know -- that's one of the pieces of evidence that we know he has been subordinated to the Drina Corps because the other piece of evidence is from Mr. Salapura and they seem to jive, to connect, the link. What does he do? He says at the bottom that this is a good opportunity now to show the rest of the world that we're treating these prisoners properly. Now, think about it. Here is the guy who is intelligence, so he must know something. I mean, if Momir Nikolic knows something, Jankovic must know something. He's on the ground, in the field working, and he sends a report and he sends it from the Bratunac Brigade, so it's slightly after midnight. So what is in his mind? What is he thinking? What does he know. What can we extract from that piece of evidence? Well, I suggest a plausible and reasonable explanation is that at that point in time Colonel Jankovic has every reason to believe that nothing is going to happen to the men. I think that is a plausible and reasonable explanation because why else would he send it unless we're going to fast forward and say, well, he probably was trying to make sure that he didn't get indicted before the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. Hardly. I don't think so. Why is that important? It's important, Your Honours, because if Colonel Jankovic doesn't know, and he's right there in the thick of things he's right at the Bratunac Brigade, how can we then say with any degree of certainty, certainty beyond a reasonable doubt, that Colonel Blagojevic knew about it, that he knew the fate of the men? I think that speaks volumes. Now, let's split the screen a little bit, because I think it's important. We really are not going to know ever probably all the facts, but we have enough and I think here's where we agree with the Prosecution that right around that time when Jankovic is in the Bratunac Brigade writing his report to the Drina Corps intelligence, over here at the SDS office, downtown Bratunac, there is a drunken Beara with a whiskey bottle calling on Deronjic, the newly appointed commissioner of Srebrenica, who is supposed to be in charge and to protect all these people and he says: I'm here to kill them. So you have those two events playing out at the same time. We don't have any evidence of Colonel Blagojevic ever being with Colonel Beara. My -- so what I'm trying suggest is this: Could it be that one plausible and reasonable explanation is that Beara is on a mission of his own, has nothing to do with Blagojevic. What Nikolic says is unclear because Deronjic says he wasn't there, Nikolic says he was, Nikolic is all over the place. And mind you, that there is also -- we also have some testimony in the afternoon or evening of the 13th where Mr. Celanovic, that lawyer -- you would ask a short question, we would get two pages of an answer, what he said. And he told us quite clearly that he took a walk in the early evening and he asked Beara: Why are these people here? He says: Well, as soon as we make some arrangements, or there wasn't enough buses, but there is an explanation right in his testimony, and he thought that that was plausible. There was no reason to think that any harm would come to these people. Now, I want to focus on this 13th because I think in my opinion - and I can't prove it beyond a shadow of a doubt, to use Mr. McCloskey's term yesterday, nor do I have to - nor do I have to, but I think if we look at all of what is going on that -- and when you factor in that we don't have any evidence, contrary to what the Prosecution is saying about killings on the 12th in Bratunac save for I think one or two witnesses, it would appear the 50 bodies or so that are found on the 14th or thereafter by the civilian protection, that must have occurred, in my opinion, late evening on the 13th going into the 14th. Also, we have the incident in Kravica in the afternoon. And here is another, I would say disconcerning [sic] incident in the final brief. There's witness 106 and 107, P106 and P107. And they give two different versions. They're not that far apart. Yesterday Mr. McCloskey touched on one, but he didn't quite, in my view, give the full picture. It would appear that one witness, 106, is under the impression that all of this happened at one time. But P107 - and this part was omitted in their brief, this part - he says that there was an incident early on in the afternoon, there's a lull, and then as it's getting dark - mind you, it's June -- or July 13th - so he says around 8.30, 9.00, he thinks that's when the incident happened. So we have two. Now, if we go backwards we have the testimony, we brought somebody who had nothing to do with the Bratunac Brigade, didn't know Colonel Blagojevic, had no reason to try to protect him or to save him or to assist him. In fact, he came here unprotected and put his face right in front of the cameras and said: I was there at the time in the vicinity - Mr. Stupar - and he said: I heard over the radio that there was an incident, and I rushed over there and he took one individual and he took him to the hospital and he heard about what had happened, about how one Muslim had tried to take a gun away from one of the Serb MUP, he was killed, and there was some killings going on out of a reaction. We really don't know. If you take that incident, it fits a little bit with what 107 is saying, that there was an incident and there was a second incident, and that's the one where everything happened. Also what's fascinating is the Prosecution came across evidence through Mr. Vasic that according to Vasic he was informed by Mr. Kovac, both of whom by the way they had an opportunity to question, and I dare say could have brought here if they wanted to, and there's a reason why I think they should have and I'll explain why, but according to Mr. Kovac he says that on the afternoon of the 13th he's driving when all of a sudden he's pulled over, he's taken over to Vlasenica, and there he goes into the headquarters and there is General Mladic. And as we all know, General Mladic had a thing about MUP, apparently he didn't like them too much. So he began to sort of verbally abuse them, and at some point the phone rang, and that's when he overheard colonel -- I mean General Mladic yelling: Kill them all, kill them all. And he says it's around 5.00 or so. So the timing, it would appear, that he's getting the news as to what happened in Kravica. Prior to that incident, we know that he stopped and spoke to some people in Sandici meadow where he told them you're going to go off, and I believe there were words to the effect of don't do anything stupid. It would appear that this was an over-reaction, that this was an over-reaction where Mladic is over-reacting over the phone, maybe he had a few beers, and probably nobody should have taken him seriously, and obviously somebody did and that was Beara. And all of a sudden things are happening. Now, the Prosecution tells us that there were incidents that happened before that. We don't know the exact timing because some of the witnesses obviously can't tell us with any degree of precision, and we don't have any independent evidence to verify it. But it could be the 13th, the exact timing we don't know. But certainly there's no linkage. There's no linkage between those incidents and the Bratunac Brigade. There's no linkage between those incidents and Colonel Blagojevic. I think that's important. And again, I want to focus us and get us all into that straightjacket called the indictment. I'm speaking in more broader terms because I want to put this matter in the perspective which I believe as the Defence for Colonel Blagojevic should be in. This is the perspective that this was not a planned genocide. There was no plan on the 11th or 12th, as the Prosecutor has indicated in the -- in their -- in the indictment, modified somewhat yesterday. And we can quibble, but you guys have the -- Your Honours have the transcript, and I trust the transcript is better than my memory. But I believe that the trip wire for all those killings is Mladic getting upset and not having the special intent to create genocide. That's my belief. I put it in my brief. I think that this was what happened afterwards, and I think we have been very straight from the beginning. We don't agree with it, we don't like it, we tried to expose it as much as we could. We think it was a horrendous experience for everybody and our heart goes out to the victims, but it doesn't mean at the end of the day we try to find somebody to pin it on because there's nobody else to pin it on, or because that one person happened to be in the area and circumstantially it would appear, if we look at nothing else, that he had to be in the vortex of hatred and therefore was engaged in all these other activities. Again, I go back because yesterday I was troubled, very troubled, by the Prosecutor insinuating that you had Mladic, Krstic, Blagojevic. My heart went out when I heard that. It was like where did that come from? Where is the evidence? And then he says, Beara, oh, couldn't hold a candle to him. Okay. I just -- where do they come up with this evidence? That's the whole problem. We have Beara in the thick of things. But what do they do? How do they try to connect Colonel Blagojevic? Well, I'll fast forward a little bit. I believe it's the 15th. Please forgive me if it's the 14th or 15th, I don't know exactly the date, but it's the intercept where -- I believe it's the 14th. Whatever. Zivanovic is mentioning Blagojevic and then Beara or Krstic is mentioning Blagojevic, but let me ask you, Your Honours, did you hear any evidence, any evidence, of any intercept with Colonel Blagojevic? Did you hear any evidence where he sent anybody to do any killings? Did you hear any evidence where there was any meetings? You hear somebody saying: Call Blagojevic. Maybe you can use his Red Berets. Is that evidence beyond a reasonable doubt? Are you willing to send somebody to essentially die in prison based on that information? Well -- and it's the 15th I'm told. But -- see, they have nothing. They're saying, well, he must have been a player because he's at - what as it? - the tip of the tongue. Well, I hope I'm at nobody's tip of the tongue because it means they can just invoke your name, and all of a sudden you can be in some joint criminal enterprise. Imagine that: Somebody uses your name and all of a sudden you're in the vortex of this joint criminal enterprise. Well, that's pretty scary, especially when there's no other evidence. And remember, Your Honours, it was on this sort of evidence that they were able to convince the Krstic Trial Chamber that the members of the Bratunac Brigade were in the killing fields of Konjevic Polje -- of Branjevo Farm. So I beg you, do not, do not rush into anything and look very carefully at the evidence. What do we know about these prisoners back then. First of all, we had Butler on the stand. And you have to hand it to him, he was on there for 11 or 12 days. I don't know how he did it. I asked him concretely: Whose prisoners were they? He wouldn't tell us. I think that's important. He couldn't tell because he didn't know and that was an honest answer. But what does the Prosecution do? They see this map of 1992 and this -- and it has its -- it is multi-coloured, kind of nice, and it's the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade. So their heart must have just, you know, exploded when they saw that. Well, we know that -- you see Zivanovic's name, he's not a general at the time. We know that -- I believe it's the Milici Brigade hasn't been formed -- the Skelani Brigade hasn't been formed. And you have Srebrenica right in the middle of the it. And there was that funny moment at the end. You know, we're trying to find a way -- I was trying, like, when can we stop using this map. I was getting tired of it. Finally it was with Mr. Karremans. And we said, okay, draw me the map. Look at this map and put me -- put the borders of where the -- the enclave was. You remember. He was reticent because there was always this dispute, where the borders are, and he thought I was trying to trick him. I said, no, just in general. There was another reason. And it would have been physically impossible under the circumstances, especially with everything changing from 1992 and 1995 to say that this was the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade. But what is it? It's a geographical region. And it fit their theory, but their theory shifted. Remember, we had Butler on the stand and Butler says, Oh yes, you can have different units sharing the same zone of responsibility. Okay. Where is that in the rules? It's not in there. Speaking of rules, remember that lovely exchange I think it was on day eight, third day of cross-examination, and it was first in the morning and I pulled out two questions and answers of his testimony. The questions were very direct. Do the rules call for a zone of responsibility for brigades? A very simple question; long answer. Same question; long answer. And so what did I do? I went home and I tried to read this. I couldn't figure out what it meant. I must tell you, a light dawned on me. I said, well, okay, why don't I take that answer and put numbers on the various words and maybe he can explain to us what those words mean so we can actually see the essence. And what I wanted to do was provide you with a tool to see that he may speak well and he may sound good but you've got to be careful because at the end of the day, as I said back then, it was gobbledegook. He didn't answer the question. Is it in the rules. It calls for a yes or a no. You can say yes and explain; you can say no and explain, but you had a long answer and there was nothing in it. And I ask you: Why? Well, we know the answer. Part of the answer is: It doesn't fit in their theory of the case because the brigade rules are very clear. Brigades have zones of defence. Zones of defence. The only ones that have a zone of responsibility is the intelligence organ and that's for a different reason. But the brigade itself, the battalions, have a zone of defence and it's a line and we saw it and it's there and it has -- you have so many yards in front or metres in front, and so many behind, and that's what you're supposed to guard. It's not a geographical region. But Mr. Butler didn't want to give it up. And again, why? Well, of course it didn't fit their theory. But you got to -- you could ask yourself, well, wait a minute. This guy is a military analyst. He was supposed to be independent. Well, he told us he was not. Remember that? That was day two, I believe. Because he said that occasionally he goes out in the field to assist on military matters. You know, he's there, sort of the military encyclopedia on hand, you know, to help out. And what did he do when he's out in the field? He's actually interrogating witnesses. Sometime playing Mutt; sometimes playing Jeff. Sometime playing good guy; sometimes playing bad guy. And we brought it out on day two, it was an evening, I vividly recall. But -- and then he said: I'm not independent. And what else did I show? I showed the portion from the Krstic trial when the Honourable Judge Wald was, in my opinion, a little bit upset with him because she was able to -- she pointed out a part of what had been going on in the OTP with respect to a particular video where there was some decisions being made whether to put that information in the report or not. If it was in the report, of course, it becomes disclosable; they have to disclose it to the Defence. And of course the theory of the Prosecution back then was: We should hold that for rebuttal. So, here is this independent analyst. Now, what did he say? He said: That wasn't really important. Why would I put that in my report? Once I decided not to put it in a report I sat back and watched this wonderful intellectual argument. Well, it sounds good. But, what was on the tape? On the tape was supposedly General Krstic saying: Kill them. That's pretty important. And the dates were not -- were within the range of the indictment. So it's not something that's way a year later or six months or a month, it's right in the period. So how could you actually sit here and say with a straight face: It wasn't important to put in the report? Mr. Butler, I dare say, was a Prosecution employee who took the stand as a Prosecution employee who has a vested interest in the outcome of this case, and that's why if you go through the -- if you go through my questioning of him and you go through his answers you see that he's not being very direct. He was slightly evasive. It was sort of the cat and the mouse. It was exhausting for me to try to pin him down because he knows the material and obviously he has a tremendous amount of stamina and he could lose me in all those documents. But I think if you look at it, and I ask you to, you will see that he's not very forthcoming in telling us exactly and answering the questions forthrightly. And this is the same individual, as I indicated, that had -- that on occasion -- there was one occasion where I told him -- I accused him of backsliding where he had given a good answer for the Defence and then once he realised where I was going he was sliding backwards, and that had to do with the functional relationship. Mr. Butler spent, I don't know, five or six years on this case. Obviously he's friends with these folks, he's got a lot vested. You lose objectivity at some point. It's not that he's a bad person. Nobody's bad over here. In fact, the world is a better place because of the Office of the Prosecution, these folks over here -- and I mean that because it is a difficult job doing what they're doing. But you can't do it so long and not lose some objectively, and that's what I'm saying. And unfortunately for Mr. Butler, he lost a whole lot of objectivity because he was just telling it the way he wanted to tell it. And again, I want to bring you back to one exchange and that had to do with the 12th, going back with Nikolic who was the coordinator on the 12th of -- in Potocari, where he said he saw all these units. And I asked

utterances.speaker: MR. BUTLER
utterances.text: Were those units there? And he said: Well, I tell you, after all those years of being in the case I had no evidence to suggest that they were there. And so then I asked him -- I think I dropped it because that's my habit. Usually I drop it and I pick it up around the bend. So I dropped it and went back. I said, you know, I've got to ask you, you know, because there was another issue that I wanted to clear up: Did you put that in your report because you had amended your report? Oh, no. Well, why not? Wasn't important. But why wasn't it important. Well, I knew you would ask me. Well, clairvoyant of him, he know what I was going to ask him. Well, what if I didn't ask him? You wouldn't have that information. Then I pointed out that at least during the Nikolic hearing Mr. McCloskey said now we know with clarity, we know beyond a shadow of a doubt. It's in the transcript. The whole point is if you know it, and it's exculpatory and it helps the Defence, why not just share it. Why? Because it might assist you in using the circumstantial evidence to see if there's another plausible and reasonable explanation. That's why. And I'm entitled to that, Colonel Blagojevic is entitled to that, we're entitled to all of that information. And we're suggesting that at least on some occasions Mr. Butler failed us. So, I threw that out. And so -- and I also suggest that these -- these sort of little vignettes demonstrate, at least to me, that when you read what he says, and please, whatever you do, check the footnotes, double-check them. But when you read what he has to say, you have to sort of take it with a grain of salt, not a tonne like Momir Nikolic, but a grain of salt. And you really have to because he makes, and I think this was commented on by the Appeals Chamber or the Trial Chamber, they talked about how he concocts these -- and he creates these inferences, he builds inference upon inference upon inference in order to figure out what's going on. And his main thing was to look at the evidence and say, well, see, people are reporting, people are filing reports, therefore the chain of command is working, circumstantial evidence. Well, we pointed out instances where those reports were not accurate. We pointed out instances where reports are going out from the Bratunac Brigade with Colonel Blagojevic's name that he's never seen, such as, for instance, on the 10th, the 10th of July when the Workers' Battalions are being asked to go up to Pribicevac and we had one witness come over here. I believe it was Tesic, Aco is his nickname, Aleksandar is his first. He came and he said: I got this order. And I turned him over to Krstic. Who signed the order? Well, the order wasn't signed by Colonel Blagojevic; it was signed in the -- it was signed in Bratunac, on the 10th. We know that Colonel Blagojevic was up in Pribicevac. But all of a sudden here are some men being mobilised and turned over to General Krstic without Colonel Blagojevic's knowledge. Speaking of knowledge, it's amazing, you know, it's difficult to really just stop at one thing because this whole case is so big. I don't know how the Prosecution did it in half a day yesterday. I commend them. But speaking of knowledge, we want to talk about what did the Bratunac Brigade commander know and how do we know what he knew? It's pretty difficult. We have to look at -- we have to look at the events. We have to look and see what's happening. And I think if we look and see what's going on in Pribicevac from 6 to 11, we get a certain picture, and the picture is that he's really not included in anything. Mladic comes and Colonel Blagojevic wants to avoid him so he goes into the woods. Then he hears he's got to go on -- there's -- a scheduled meeting is in Srebrenica, so he walks down there. Yesterday, the Prosecution: Well, maybe he met him, maybe he didn't. He's not on the video. It's as if, if we don't have the evidence, it must be true. Well -- but what do you see? You see someone who is really not a player, so to speak in the vernacular. He's really a man of no importance, just like Nikolic, although Nikolic wants to be a man of importance, hence why he's a guest at the UN Detention Unit. But you don't see anybody reporting to Colonel Blagojevic. You don't see Nikolic writing any reports to him. You don't see him being invited to any meetings. Remember, there was a meeting in the Bratunac Brigade on the morning of the 12th. Who was called over there? Members of the government. Was Colonel Blagojevic called? No. There was a meeting on the 12th at the Hotel Fontana. Was Colonel Blagojevic called? No. Was he consulted? No. Well, one or two of his buses were used, Trisic was contacted. But we had that functional relationship. Trisic was very clear: I didn't contact Colonel Blagojevic. He didn't have to because what was being asked was not really anything nefarious, number one, and number two, it was not stripping the Bratunac Brigade of its resources as Mr. Butler would have us believe, at least with the fuel. Because that's what Mr. Butler looked at. And if you just look at the receipts, you might come to that conclusion, hence the dangers of circumstantial evidence. But nobody's reporting. What is Colonel Blagojevic doing? Let's get to that answer -- question. Well, remember we've had -- there is this event to capture Srebrenica. Srebrenica falls on the 11th. Colonel Blagojevic is at no commander meetings, nobody sees him. We know, at least from one of the witnesses, that he hitchhikes a ride back to Bratunac sometime at night, the night of the 11th. On the 12th he's out there visiting his troops. What should a commander do? Now, the Prosecutor would have you believe that he's out there in order to use his troops in order to push the column in order to capture and kill them. That's how I read what they're saying. First of all, let's be fair. This column did not have a thousand armed men, as I believe it's pointed out somewhere in their brief; it was more like 5 or 6.000. Number one. Number two, it was an army on the run; they were on the go. Nobody knew exactly where it was going, but it was in RS-held territory. They were heading -- we know now that they were heading towards Zvornik. On the other side you had the 2nd Corps and they're trying to link up, with Zvornik being right on the edge. Butler says on the stand, morning of the 12th the commanders think that the 28th Division, because Karremans didn't know where they were, were probably held up in the Bandera triangle. Remember? That was a triangle where the DutchBat were held prisoners by the 28th Division. That was forbidden land for the DutchBat because that's where all the smuggling of the weapons were coming in. It turned out everybody was wrong. But according to Butler on the morning of the 12th, that's where they think. Now we do have a Zvornik Brigade -- in the Zvornik area by the fourth -- where the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade is located we have a sighting and it appears, they can correct me if I'm wrong, it's somewhere around 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning, somewhere around there, that Major Obrenovic at the time learns about it. Even there at that point in time nobody really -- at least at that area, nobody knew the significance, the importance. But we do know one thing: They left the Bratunac area. Because you have the Bratunac Brigade on one side, the Milici Brigade on the other. And they left -- and we have testimony -- we brought the commanders, we brought the commanders here and what do they all say? There was no battle activity, they went about their business. First of all, the terrain itself, there -- it was a natural buffer zone, and there was no need for them to engage because once they saw the size, there weren't about to engage them. They let them pass. But the searching of the terrain, even Butler admits that this is a proper military activity, nothing nefarious about it. There was no such thing as trying to chase out and hunt down and kill. And also, who can forget those lovely witnesses that we brought in from the 2nd Battalion, was it the 1st Company I believe -- 2nd Company, and they told us about having to go to Budak. A lot of facts, it's tough to remember all of it. But he's going to Budak and the one guy says, you know, you see him in a photograph, he has his rifle and as I indicated sort of like the kid that's running away from home. He's holding it on his shoulder with a little food bag on the end, and what does he say? I'm told that I'm going on an informational walk with my friends. The guy's about 60 years old. Lovely guy. And what does he do? He says, you know, I walk over, I see some friends, I see the Muslim population. Then I head up to the hills, it was like a hike. And then once I got there I was told to go home. How did you search the terrain? Everybody was asked that question. Right? In single file on the asphalt road searching the terrain. And I believe, Mr. President, you even asked that question of one or two witnesses. What does that tell us? What does that tell us? First of all, they didn't even know how to search the terrain even if they wanted to and they had to. Second of all, they really didn't have any orders to go out there and chase and sort of herd any stragglers, or capture and kill. Then we heard testimony that half the time they weren't even carrying out these orders. That's the extent of the Bratunac Brigade and the commander was out there at least trying to make sure that nobody would come into harm's way. And isn't that what you want a commander to do, to check up after battle just to make sure your men are okay. And remember it was the commander of the 3rd Battalion, Mr. Zekic, he said that he had some problems with his men because his men were from the Srebrenica area and they had been looking at their town for the last two or three years and they were dying to get -- to go visit their homes and he had a hard time keeping them back and his commander told them: Just stay, just hold -- hold put. And any searching orders that they got were incremental, and that was confirmed by the Prosecution's own witness, (redacted) I get the B's and the D's mixed occasionally. But (redacted) indicated that he had been given some orders to move slightly ahead, which he did. And then, as Mr. McCloskey pointed out the following day, I think it was, that there had to be this pep talk between -- with General Mladic in order to motivate the men. We know that on the 14th -- the 13th by the way, we also see -- we have witnesses that said that Colonel Blagojevic again went to the terrain, visited some of his folks, visited his ill mother. And anybody who lives in that part of the world knows that it's not like, Hello mom, I hope you're okay, and then you leave. That's not how it's done. But he goes and visits his mother who lives nearby. But he's basically checking up on his men. And also he has orders to put together some men to go off towards Milici, and he's going to send his Chief of Staff Novica Pajic to do that. On the 14th he gets orders to search the terrain and he marks where they should search, what they should do. We had Mr. Gavric who came and he was the gentleman who had to be sent to Zvornik. Remember that the Zvornik Brigade by this point in time was in trouble because all of a sudden they realised they couldn't handle what was happening with all -- the column coming their way plus all the other activity that they were involved in that they shouldn't have been involved in. But in any event Colonel Blagojevic was ordered to send some men. And what did Mr. Gavric say? Because remember he's the guy with the rocket platoon or whatever the name of the platoon is. But he says: My men are not soldiers in the field. We don't walk in the field and carry guns. We're sort of correct and shoot. And now I'm getting orders to go to the Zvornik Brigade to go to some territory I don't know, my men are not equipped. But the commander says: Go there and I'll bring you right back. Stop and think about that for a second. The commander has an obligation to send some men so he does that and he tells them: I'm going to get somebody else. I just need to send you over there. They go there, they report on the night of the 14th, and they come back on the 15th and he says nothing happened. The next day there was another group. And you heard Zoran Kovacevic talk about somewhat of a horrifying experience that he had, that because they got lost, one person was lost because the size of his boots were too big, and they lost him and for two days they were out there not knowing what would happen, but they don't engage the enemy.
