They certainly don't get involved in any killings. But what am I trying to show here? That Colonel Blagojevic is acting according to orders that are proper and normal. You don't hear him on any intercepts. Now, the Prosecution says that he's working in the shadows. Okay. What does that mean? Well, to me it means that if there's no evidence on you it must mean you have a guilty mind and you have been acting guiltily, but because you know that somebody's watching so you're covering your tracks. That's what they're saying. We don't have the evidence, so he must be guilty. If we had the evidence we would show you, or since we can't show you, we want you to infer that. Where is the evidence? It's not there. On the 15th, we have that piece of evidence -- oh, Your Honours, it's 1.30. I can keep going, but I think we need that little break. Now if I can squeeze an extra half hour this afternoon, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to any change of the rules at this point. I think everyone knows the rules, and I think we should stick by them, so he gets the full amount of time that you designated earlier..

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Obviously my generosity of allowing him 50 more pages on his final brief is not being returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's discuss this matter when you resume in the afternoon. We will resume at 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before resume could I ask a question to Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic, how long do you think your cross-argument will last?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have so far written about 50 pages of our closing argument. While I was rehearsing, the average was about four minutes a page, which would amount to about 200 minutes that we would like to use up tomorrow for our closing argument. I think that amounts to three hours or just over three hours. I think that would be sufficient time for us in view of the arguments put forward by the OTP yesterday. That would be suffice for us to say to present our position without repeating any of the things that we have already submitted in your final brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stojanovic. Here's a question for you: Would you please lend 30 minutes to your colleague, Mr. Karnavas, for him to finish his closing argument today?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I have already informed the registrar prior to our continuation today, our Defence will gladly give those 30 minutes over to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Well, I believe that Mr. Karnavas should finish his closing argument today, that is within one and a half hours. And frankly speaking, Mr. Karnavas, I believe that your closing argument could be more concise and sometimes I found that you just got carried away by your thought or your strategy, and there are some unnecessary remarks or even personal attacks to the other party which I don't believe is necessary. As for tomorrow, tomorrow morning I believe that we could finish the closing argument by Mr. Stojanovic. And in the afternoon we will have the rebuttal and the rejoinder session. I understand that the Prosecution has two accused to deal with, so we'll give the Prosecution extra 15 minutes to deal with the two closing arguments. Then each party will have 30 minutes for the rejoinder. I believe that the scope of the rejoinder should be within the scope of the rebuttal, which means that that is not an opportunity for the parties to re-present their case. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We want to thank the Jokic team for their generosity and I'll proceed. I want to go back to the 12th and the 13th and -- of July. And if it seems that I'm attacking the Prosecution, it is that I am attacking their case because it would appear that there are other reasonable and plausible explanations that we need to look at based on the evidence. And so I don't think it's appropriate for us to place a blind eye to the microscope when we look at the evidence. Now, on the -- we -- I talked a little bit on the 12th of July and I spoke about what Colonel Blagojevic was doing on that particular day. We heard testimony that on the evening he came back from the field and that he had someone from the brigade that was with him to go check on the prisoners that were being held at the school, at the gymnasium, I believe. And that he had given that individual specific instructions, that is, to talk to the MPs that were there to make sure that they would conduct themselves appropriately. The Prosecution has dismissed that witness outright as not being truthful as to that part, although they like the rest of the part that is Colonel Blagojevic speaking to the witness. Again, the bipolarity of the way they look at Defence witnesses. When they like something, he's credible; when they don't like something because it's exculpatory, the evidence cuts against Blagojevic. Now, we have another witness that goes and visits them on the 13th. And again the question that I think has never been answered by the Prosecutor, because it's their duty not ours, how did the prisoners get there and who transferred the prisoners there, who was responsible for those prisoners? They make this general accusation that everything in the town of Bratunac is run by Blagojevic. That's what they did yesterday. That he was about the civilian government in a sense, if you look at their argument quite carefully, although there's nothing there to suggest that. We don't know exactly who sent them there, but it would appear from this one witness that was brought in by the Prosecution that obviously Mr. Blagojevic learned of it, learned that some of the MPs were guarding them. And you have to remember what the function of the MPs are. What are their functions? Yesterday the Prosecution insinuated that because some of them were guarding -- were on the entourage of General Mladic they knew about the forcible transfer and they automatically knew also about this genocidal plan which was on the 11th, 12th, or 13th. That's what was the gist of it. So we don't know. But it would appear that at least upon learning that his men are guarding some prisoners, and that -- you would seem -- that would seem somewhat innocuous because it comes within their domain that he did the appropriate thing. The next morning we have a witness who said that he went to check up on the men -- on the prisoners over there to see if any of them needed any medicine. We know that he wasn't a doctor, he was more like a medic. He carried some pills. Again, the Prosecution would have you believe that that elderly gentleman that came here was nothing but an apologist or someone who was simply here because he wanted to be kind to Colonel Blagojevic and obviously was untruthful. Imagine all these people coming from Bratunac just to be untruthful; that's what the Prosecution is insinuating. We, on the other hand, suggest that this gentleman who had nothing to gain by coming here was speaking the truth, and it would appear again that Colonel Blagojevic was trying to do the decent thing to make sure that, you know, nothing was awry, nothing was going bad, happening over there. Again it fits in what we believe is the evidence. Because we believe that nothing really happens until it's the evening of the 13th going into the 14th. Although in the afternoon of the 13th it would appear that you have all these special units that are doing all sorts of things in and around Potocari and elsewhere. Under whose command they are, nobody knows. Whether they are Drina Corps, Main Staff, MUP, they have different uniforms. We heard from Mr. Celanovic. He told us about what he was able to observe. So it's rather unclear. Now, the Prosecutor in their brief -- and I don't mean to be attacking them but again I have to bring it to the Court's attention, they would have us believe that the first bus went to Orahovac on the night of the 13th. So what they're trying to imply there is that the killing operation began on the evening of the 13th to Orahovac, therefore we can impute some sort of knowledge to Colonel Blagojevic. I would suggest because I don't have much time that you look at paragraphs 256 and 263. And if we look then at the testimony of the one witness, it's on page 1.277, and then another transcript of 6.741 to 6.746, we see that in essence nobody arrived in Orahovac on the night of the 13th, as they would have us believe, but rather it was the morning. At worse, you have two conflicting pieces of evidence that you have to look at, but it certainly doesn't comport with what the Prosecution would have us believe. Again, what I'm suggesting -- and it's not an attack on the Prosecution but there's another reasonable alternative explanation that I think we should not put our blind eye to the microscope in looking at it. Now, the night of the 13th we know that there were members of the Bratunac Brigade military police that were there guarding the buses. We know that Bratunac was full of people -- full of prisoners. Who was bringing them in it's rather unclear. Again, it's not our job to prove it. It's their job. They've had eight years. They've had the resources. They're able to go back and forth and find these things out. Keep in mind that we brought the witnesses here. Well, they want to imply that somehow the Bratunac Brigade military police were engaged in all this nefarious activities. My question is: Why didn't they bring them here? Why didn't they question them? They were there, they were open. And as you recall, I asked each and every one of them: Were you hiding someplace, were you available if they wanted to question you, to ask you what you were doing. So they were there. And why did they come here? Because they had nothing to hide. Now, you've been to Bratunac; it's a small place. It's easy to say today, well, it's impossible not to have known, because that's what the Prosecution's case is all about. They have no concrete evidence. It's impossible not to have known. Everybody in town knew. They wanted to bring in one witness, P30, who committed perjury when he testified the first time. To come in to admit to committing perjury and also to say all these other killings were going on in the stadium. Again, I suggest that even though the town was rather small, you had all these buses, you had all these prisoners, it's hard to say today looking back exactly what those people knew at that particular time. And to say that those people knew for sure that they were going to be killed or at least Colonel Blagojevic knew they were going to be killed. And again I focus you back to Colonel Jankovic. If he didn't know how is it that Blagojevic would know and where is the evidence? That's what I'm focusing on. Where is the evidence that the Prosecution should show us something other than to say we know they were killed later on, therefore they must have had knowledge. On the morning of the 14th we know that Popovic of the Drina Corps orders I believe it's witness 138 and Mr. Petrovic to lead sort of the convoy. Now, who is Popovic? He is security of the Drina Corps. Is there any evidence, any evidence at all, that he had sought the permission of Colonel Blagojevic to issue that order? No. But we do know that there is a close link, a close association, between Popovic and Nikolic. We do know even from Your Honour's last question that the military police were taking their orders from Nikolic and they were responding to him, it would appear, which is why Colonel Blagojevic had to ask Nikolic to come up to Trnovo, I believe, to issue an order to his men, because they were responding to him, because Nikolic behaved as if the military police were his troops to do as he pleased. Now, yesterday I was a little troubled. I didn't object because I didn't think that it would be appropriate, although in hindsight I should have. But the Prosecutor accused the Defence of somehow saying that the troops were being stolen. Now, I don't know where they came up with that idea. We have never said that anybody was stealing any troops. We've never said that Beara was stealing troops from the Bratunac Brigade. They would have you believe that because then it doesn't fit in with the functional relationship and then you also see these intercepts. And again that was covered by Mr. Butler who said: You see, Beara is calling Krstic to use so-and-so's men, therefore he just -- he's not reaching out to the troops. There is an exchange between myself and Mr. Butler, and we agree on that, because there is no functional relationship. And there lies the difference. The military police, even though they are an asset of the brigade commander -- and we've never shied away from that. We've never said anything other than that. We in fact go by the rules. Even though they are an asset of the brigade commander they do take their orders, it would appear, on a day-to-day basis from the security organ. Here in the Bratunac Brigade you had one individual who wore both hats, security and intelligence, who was rather imposing in some ways, who had been around. And as I've indicated and as the evidence shows, was more or less a self-manager. So who is to tell whether on the morning of the 14th Nikolic, without getting permission from Colonel Blagojevic, agreed with Popovic to have the men escort this convoy up towards Orahovac. Is there any evidence that Popovic or Beara or Nikolic consulted with Colonel Blagojevic? There's zero. Whose responsibility is it to prove that? Not the Defence -- at least not in this system. Now, where is Orahovac? And I think that's something that you need to appreciate. Orahovac is on its way towards Zvornik where you would have the line to cross over the border. The Prosecution would have you believe because we now know that there were killings in Orahovac that they all knew in advance that they were going there in order to kill all those folks. In hindsight you may say, yeah, fine, because we know the killings, so therefore you somehow can make that connection. There's no evidence but that's what they say. And I'm looking for the evidence. What about another plausible and reasonable explanation. Could it be that they had no reason to believe that these people, these prisoners, were going to be killed? Could it be that they believed that they were going to be exchanged because that would be the appropriate place for them to be exchanged or could it be that they thought that they were on their way to Bijeljina where there was a prison. Bijeljina is about 20 kilometres if you keep going, so it's in the same direction. Where is the independent evidence to establish that they knew? Where is there any evidence other than looking back and saying, well, we've had the murders, therefore they must have known. When do we have the first killings in Orahovac? We have them in the afternoon or the evening, the evening of the 14th, not in the morning. They don't see anything when they drop them off. They take them and then they head back. Now, we do have that one entry in the logbook of a patrol, a patrol means two, members of the Bratunac Brigade in that area and the date escapes me. I believe it's the 16th or 17th, somewhere around there. Well, I ask you: Did they bring any witnesses? Did they bring anybody from the Bratunac Brigade military police to establish that, because that's their job, that's their responsibility. They have the resources, they have the burden of proof. They have the burden of proof. Well, Your Honour, I certainly don't have the burden of proof of proving that that occurred. If they're just going to show an entry in a logbook and then ask you to make a finding beyond a reasonable doubt that they were there in order to say because they were there, they participated in the killings, and therefore Colonel Blagojevic should die in prison, I think that's an awfully long stretch. If they're going to make that accusation, they have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But this repeated reference to "die in prison," is just inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 32 years, Your Honour. 32 years is what he asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think I remind you of that -- at least you have some unnecessary remarks, and we have heard and we understand what you are doing to present to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I just wanted to remind the Court about the amount of time. It was 32 years. It wasn't a small amount of time that they are asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have been reminded for several times already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. With respect to the separate chain of command I want to talk a little bit about that. I touched on it earlier. You do have the testimony of General Keserovic. Again, the Prosecution spoke to General Keserovic, they had access to his notebook. General Keserovic's name pops up on the July 17th, 1995, when he's asked by General Mladic to take over when Colonel Blagojevic goes off to Zepa about that searching of the terrain. We heard from him. But who is General Keserovic? He was intimately knowledgeable about the security organ. We brought him here because we thought after the Prosecution had spoke to him and had provided some information and in light of General Mladic's instruction that it might be useful for you to hear from General Keserovic. And I invite your close scrutiny and attention. And I ask you to look at part of his testimony because I think that it's rather telling with respect to the use of the military police by the security organ. It's in the testimony. Again, because of the time, I don't want to go into it. As you can see, we have some documents that I was prepared to go through. But again, it's in the testimony, General Keserovic. And he talks specifically also about this separate chain of command and he said he thought it was two-thirds/one-third. Then we showed him the document to see whether that was the one that he was referring to, and he said yes, 80/20. Then there was this exchange about what is counter-intelligence and he gave us some kind of a definition. But when you look at that whole definition and you look at the way it's applied and who comes up with it and who decides what's counter-intelligence, it appears that the security makes that determination themselves. It's sort of a moving target. It could be whatever they feel or think it is. Obviously if they are engaged in what they believe is counter-intelligence they are not going to inform their commanders. And in fact, on cross-examination Mr. McCloskey asked

utterances.speaker: MR. KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, when in doubt, you've got to tell your commander. And Keserovic said: No, it's the opposite. When in doubt you don't tell the commander. It's all in that testimony. What am I saying here? I think you need to look at that kind of information and try to understand about how the security organ functioned and how it functioned during this period of time, during a wartime, and it would appear that with this instruction from General Mladic that the security organ sort of took on a life of its own and were operating perhaps outside the rules in certain matters. Now, I agree with the Prosecution that you have Beara asking if he can take troops away from here or there. But again, there's no functional relationship, and that's the key. You need that functional relationship. And what we are suggesting, and what we have suggested, is that members of the Bratunac Brigade military police, if they were used to guard, if they were used to escort, albeit they were not involved at any time in any activities and had no knowledge to know what was going on, in spite of all the by the Prosecution that they were being directed by Momir Nikolic, outside the knowledge of the Bratunac Brigade commander. And we see also that during this period there's a lot of ordering around. We see Mladic, for instance, ordering Mr. Stanisevac [phoen] with the APC, tells him to go towards Potocari. He ends up having to go to Bratunac to get some fuel and then to fix up the APC. You have Mladic ordering the shelling directly. No knowledge of the commander, bypassing the commander completely. Can Mladic do this? Of course he can. But when Mladic issues that order, who's responsible? Because at that point in time, it would be our submission, that once Mladic issues the order, that individual is acting under Mladic's order. And if the brigade commander is unaware of that activity, you can't later on hold him responsible for it. But our contention is that they did not act improperly. You have no shelling of civilians. And it's called, as I'm reminded, the unity of command. That's the unity of command principle. But it seems that during that period, contrary to what Mr. Butler wanted us to believe, this was not the JNA; this was the VRS. Big difference. This was an army that was put together. You had some officers who were trained at the top, then you had reservist officers filling the mid-ranks, and you had the citizen soldier who was two weeks on and two weeks off. That's what you basically had. You didn't have the professional JNA army. And you can't compare one with the other. The only thing that you can do is look at the JNA rules and say: For the most part, they had been adopted. But once you do that, you have to take the rest of it, which is the military doctrine. Now, that's the part we don't like, so we don't look at. And I suggest you have to, you must, because they're inseparable. Now, I want to go on to the 15th and the 16th of July, because there was some talk about a suggestion that was made by Colonel Milanovic. He made that suggestion to General Krstic. And it would appear -- we don't have the order itself, unless I'm mistaken, but I've never seen an order by General Krstic to Colonel Blagojevic, but we do have the interim daily combat report of the 16th. And so I think we can say: Well, based on that -- I mean, there is where you could look at circumstantial evidence and draw some conclusions. I don't have a problem with that sort of circumstantial evidence. But there you could say: All right. It would appear that Milanovic's suggestion was accepted by General Krstic. But what does the Prosecution do yesterday? And again, I'm not trying to attack the Prosecution, but I have to attack their position; I'm defending. I know no other way of doing it. What they're trying to suggest is that because they chose Colonel Blagojevic, that is some sort of indicia that he was the man, and only man available for that job. That's what I heard yesterday. But if you look at the circumstances and you look at the reasons why Colonel Blagojevic is recommended, is because there was nobody else available. Far cry from: He is it. He is the most competent individual. Nobody else is there. You know, that's not the case. Also, you have to keep in mind that on the same day, on the 16th, he gets an order to mobilise for Zepa. Now, look at the two tasks that he has. One is to go and check up and perhaps coordinate among the various units that are doing the searching operation. And again, there's nothing. There's not one single shred of evidence that would show that that searching operation that he was being asked to coordinate was conducting any illegal activities. But be that as it may, he has that. And then he has to mobilise virtually his entire brigade to go to a foreign place, because basically that's what we're talking about, to a location in Zepa where they're going to be engaged in combat. And I think you cannot lose sight of that. So if you put them on the balancing scale, where would the commander place his time? This is the same commander that visited his troops on the 12th and the 13th. Is it not reasonable and plausible that he would spend his time mobilising? Because this is not something that you can just give an order and it just happens. And I think when you look at the Bratunac Brigade it's hardly a Swiss clock. Things are not working that smoothly. We do have one witness - we brought one witness from Serbia, if you may recall - who said that: They did not carry out this order. They went all the way to Konjevic Polje, I believe. It's DP106. And then they came back, and basically they concentrated on the mobilisation process. But again, I asked you to look at the two arguments. The Prosecution is saying: This is an order from Mladic; therefore, it's going to get done, and this is why he's picked. And what I'm suggesting is: He's got two orders at the same time, one where he has to mobilise his troops, where they're going to go into combat, where you have the risk of losing the lives of your soldiers, the most precious commodity that a brigade has, versus going and visiting and giving some tasks. And I think there's another reasonable and plausible explanation. Again, I know that you know this, but I have to keep repeating: I don't have to prove this; they do. We do know that we have testimony from Mico Gavric, who was there, I believe, on the 17th. He was the one that was out in the field. He said that he was asked to coordinate, that MUP -- we had -- remember Mr. Dusko Jevic, aka Stalin. He was out there. And there's some disagreement as to who was subordinated to whom or whether they were working, coordinating, side by side. Dusko Jevic, who is MUP, obviously it would be much better for him to say that he was subordinated to the Bratunac Brigade in case something happened to any of the men that they ad captured that day. That's a natural reaction. Mr. Gavric says his orders were, one, from Colonel Blagojevic: Make sure nothing happens to anybody that is captured, make sure that the Geneva Conventions are complied with. That's number one. Number two, he was there to coordinate. And if you may recall when Major Obrenovic was on the stand, we were able to show a part of his statement where he had been questioned by the Prosecutor on a similar instance, where we had been asked whether MUP was subordinated to the Zvornik Brigade as they were searching. And he said: No. We were working side by side. And Mr. McCloskey asked him: Well, that's kind of dangerous, don't you think, you know? And he says: Yes, but that's how it was. So it's not an out-of-the-ordinary situation. So I'm not asking you to sort of fantasize about something that might be done. We have a concrete example from a Prosecution cooperating witness, based on evidence that we know. So I'm suggesting you have another plausible and reasonable explanation that they were working -- they were coordinating. But what does Mico Gavric say? He says on that particular day they captured some children. He took personal custody of the children. We know that they were all -- they were treated well and they were taken to safety. The men -- it's quite unclear as to who captured them, but it turns out that they were in the hands of MUP and taken to Konjevic Polje. The question was asked of him: Why didn't you take them to the Bratunac Brigade or to Bratunac? And the answer was: Where they were captured and the location and the terrain - and you have to appreciate the terrain; you've been there - but where they were captured, it was right by the intersection. You have that intersection that goes Konjevic Polje-Bratunac, and then it goes Milici one way and it goes to Zvornik the other way. So they were captured right around there. So it made sense. And the next day, Mico Gavric said that he saw the men. He indicated that he had no reason to believe that any harm would come to them. If Mico Gavric was this sort of demon, as -- you know, possessed within this vortex of hatred, as we heard, why would he try to save the children? Why not kill them as well? I submit that Mico Gavric's testimony is extremely credible. And I suggest that he shows another side of the Bratunac Brigade, and that is that Colonel Blagojevic had strict instructions to his men that they were to behave accordingly. And I want to fast-forward a couple of months from then, September, October; it's unclear. But if you may recall, they learned that there were some Muslims in a hill, hiding. And of course, you have to appreciate that nobody knows whether they're armed or not armed, what they're there for. But Sreten Petrovic is asked to go out there and check out the situation, and he does, and he captures them and he brings them to Bratunac. They share breakfast together. They even give him three rakijas, according to the one survivor that we saw. That was DP104. And they were treated appropriately. So again, here's another example. If there was this vortex of hatred, where there -- everybody's just a killing machine because of the ravages of war, why do we have these examples? And we saw the one person who came in, and he said he was treated properly, "correctly," was the word. And we're grateful for the fact that he came in and told us his story. So let me move on. We have -- I want to speak a little bit about the burials -- the reburials and the burials. With the burials, we have testimony with respect to the civilian protection. The Prosecution would have us believe that everybody's working under the military, or if not, they're working together and inseparably, and also that somehow the Bratunac Brigade might be connected with all of these activities. Because we do know that there are some members who are in the civil protection who at the same time - at least one of them - had been mobilised with the Workers' Battalion, who is then called to the civil protection. We tried to establish through evidence where the lines were and who was issuing the orders when, who had the competencies. Needless to say, there's not one shred of evidence that would demonstrate that Colonel Blagojevic was involved in any capacity whatsoever with the civil protection. There was one witness who testified, if you might recall -- he was a truck driver. He was working in a mine. And he was on the list. And so on direct examination, the Prosecution was trying to establish that he's a member of the Bratunac Brigade; therefore, you can draw some conclusions from that. But if you recall, we were able to demonstrate on cross-examination that he had been placed on the list because -- well, first of all, he was the only male survivor in his family - and the policy was during that period for the male survivors not to be on the front line - and at the same time was able to put his name on the list so that they could get the groceries or the subsidies. And finally, remember when I showed him the document and it turned out that it was his wife's signature that had been collecting all of that? And then he came clean and indicated that, yes, he was just there on name alone. And there was at least one other witness that said the same thing. And in fact, when he came in and the Prosecution confronted him with the list, he found his own name, with somebody else's signature, who apparently was taking out groceries, or supplies, based on having his name there. Somebody had signed it -- got his name on the list and was signing to get stuff out. There's absolutely -- we heard testimony from Mirkovic, who talked about when he was mobilised and what he was tasked to do. You hear absolutely no testimony from that gentleman whether there's any connection between him and the Bratunac Brigade or him and Colonel Blagojevic. Now, on the reburials we have some evidence. One, there is the notebook of Momir Nikolic where he says that he was at a meeting and he made the announcement that he's conducting asanacija on behalf of the Main Staff. Now, let's stop and pause for a second. When did this asanacija begin? Because right around that period, September going into October, we know that Colonel Blagojevic is engaged in moving the Bratunac Brigade from Bratunac to Trnovo. So he's going back and forth. But more importantly this is a Main Staff operation. Probably Beara is running the operation with Popovic. We know that Popovic is involved because apparently there are some petrol receipts. This is an operation from the highest levels. And of course in order for Nikolic, because he's being tasked directly, he apparently uses members of the Bratunac Brigade military police. There's not one single piece of evidence that Colonel Blagojevic issued any orders with regard to that. However, I think we can draw an inference that based on this document that at least Colonel Blagojevic was put on notice that this activity was going on, at the very minimum we can draw that conclusion. And I believe there was also testimony that -- from witnesses that said they could smell the odour as the trucks went by. So it would be very difficult to be there and not know that activity. Question -- these are assets, the military police are assets of the Bratunac Brigade. To what extent did Colonel Blagojevic have the ability to say no to the Main Staff, that's number one. Number two, all right, he learns that there is this operation going on for the reburials, which I believe the Court has already found that is not a natural and foreseeable consequence of the earlier activities but it would be sort of aiding and abetting after the fact. Obviously under the rules then existing the brigade commander had a responsibility to launch an investigation and to punish, if necessary. But as you may recall, I began with stating the law because, one, you cannot ask the commander to do the impossible. What are his -- the means that are available? And here again I want to draw the Court's attention that we brought the one witness -- the right witness I should say, that should have been brought to tell us about the means available at the time in order to launch an investigation and to prosecute. He was the military prosecutor at that time. We also brought an investigator who was working with the military police in Bijeljina, and he would be the person that would be conducting -- carrying out the investigations at the behest of the Prosecution or investigative judge, Mr. Gajic. Now, we went through the rules a little bit, and I think this is important - and again I stressed it earlier, I want to stress it again - I asked both of them, but more particularly the prosecutor, could somebody come in and make an anonymous complaint. And the answer was: No, I had to take the name down. All right. And who would conduct the investigation? It would be the security organ. All right. Then we sort of looked at the rules and we figured out -- tried to figure out where would Colonel Blagojevic, for instance, assuming he wanted to launch an investigation, where would he go? Well, he can't directly investigate Momir Nikolic. He would have to go and file a complaint or ask for assistance from the Drina Corps assistant commander for security, that's Mr. Popovic. Is there any doubt that Mr. Popovic was involved in these activities? Hardly. We see his fingerprints everywhere. So imagine asking Popovic to investigate Nikolic for the activities that perhaps Nikolic was involved as a result of getting orders from Popovic. All right. Kind of difficult. Would you say impossible? Well, I think so. Well, who else was involved? Beara. Where would you go -- who would you ask to investigate Beara when you find out that Beara was in town, he's responsible, he's the one who came and took all these -- the prisoners on the morning of the 14th and issued all these orders. Where would you go? Well, can you imagine asking Beara to investigate himself for the killings that he was doing? You can't. You could go to Mladic I guess. I think it's pretty clear that General Mladic was probably at the top of some of this activity. And we're talking about a lieutenant colonel at the time, and we're asking today looking back at The Hague where we have witness protection for our witnesses. We fly them in, nobody knows where they're staying, they're under complete protection. Or if you have a cooperating witness, we give them witness protection, they can live in a nice country, have a job, their families. They have all this protection. Basically a new identity. Well, Your Honour, I think it's important, because if you're going to ask somebody to risk their life in this -- today, in our environment, we say it's okay. We'll provide you with those sorts of resources and assistance because of what you're going to tell us, because we realise that you're placing your life in jeopardy. Think back now what it must have been like during the war years. If we worry about the safety of those people today, why would we not worry about their safety back then when it was sort of the Wild Wild West when you had people going around doing as they pleased. You had sort of these paramilitaries. So I ask you: Would it have been possible under the circumstances back then knowing what we know now of how things operated back then, and would it have been reasonable to ask somebody to go and try to forfeit his life or the life of his family to report and to launch an investigation of activities that have already occurred? I think that's what the important aspect of it is. In my brief I mentioned that in essence you have sort of a self-defence. You're trying to defend yourself or defend others, and that's why you're not taking that positive step, assuming that you knew and you needed to take that positive step. Or you could -- it's an imperfect -- it's not a complete defence, and that would be the defence of necessity. That's why in my brief I made reference to that. Because I think you have to look at the facts as they existed back then. And that's why I keep focusing your attention to the facts as they existed back then, especially when you're trying to figure out what everybody knew at the time. The Prosecution, as I continue to say, makes these generalisations. Basically when you look at things back then and you see his position, he knew, he must have known, he had to have known, if you see that his name is being mentioned on intercepts, that means that he must have been involved. And I say: Where is the hard evidence? Where is it? And if you're going to try to draw some inferences you at least have to eliminate all the other reasonable and plausible conclusions. And that must be the only reasonable and plausible conclusion that you must be able to prove beyond a reasonable doubt before you can reach it. If I may have a moment. It's almost finished. It looks like I won't need the extra time, but I do want to talk a little bit about Nikolic one last time because there is a rather interesting exchange. Again, I want to focus the Court's attention. We have been very critical, as you know, of the final brief by the Prosecution. It's hard not to be -- not to criticise somebody when you're critical of their -- of what they've done. It's not personal, it's professional. But I want to focus on paragraph 341 of their final brief. Because they make a statement with respect to documents being destroyed, and I think it's rather important. It says towards the bottom of the page, page 125, it says: "The Bratunac Brigade documents in this case make scant reference to the murder operation. However, Captain Momir Nikolic testified that he had destroyed a significant number of Bratunac Brigade documents after the war, including the Bratunac Brigade documents most likely to include such references." And they point to -- there's a footnote, 1047. Well, I was rather curious about that, and of course 1047 goes to some of the transcript. But then there was an interesting exchange between Momir Nikolic and Judge Vassylenko. And Judge Vassylenko was trying to get Momir Nikolic to answer a question about these documents. You know, what documents exactly did he destroy. Were these documents that were orders by the Bratunac Brigade commander that would somehow implicate Colonel Blagojevic? Were these personal documents? Because after all we know that he was a security officer and even by the Prosecution's own admissions, they tend -- those security officers tend to sort of be very guarded when it came to having documents where they had vital information. And I don't want to read the entire exchange, but on page 2.366, Judge Vassylenko asked: "Can you describe the documents you've destroyed?" A pretty concrete question. Answer: "I can, Your Honour. Among others, there was my diary which contained everything that was going on while in the period while I was in the army, by dates, times, names. Also there were many names, many pieces of information that were handwritten, not typed out. So this was the type of documents involved, diary, my notes, my opinions, et cetera. That's the kind of documents that were there that I had burned and left." "Q. Did you destroy any documents containing orders from your superiors and documents signed by yourself?" "A. No, Your Honours. Here on this list it can be seen that I left those orders that came to me because I think there was no need to destroy those documents." I think he cuts across a little bit -- cuts against, I should say, what the Prosecution is insinuating that somehow we don't have the orders because there was Momir Nikolic destroying all these documents, including perhaps vital documents that would tie Colonel Blagojevic into the thick of things. Just let me wind up with a couple of things. I've talked about being in this straightjacket, which is the indictment. It's kind of hard to stay in that straightjacket when the Prosecution's case is all outside it, at least that's our opinion. When they make references to 1992, when they make references to what the RS plan was and they tried to infer knowledge, it's rather difficult. When they talk about May 25, 1995, which is not in the indictment, it's not charged, they make -- they spend a considerable amount of time talking about it. For you to infer somehow that day one, he comes in, takes over, and the first thing he does is shell. They don't tell you the rest of the story, which is it's not his order and it's a retaliation because of the NATO bombings. He has nothing to do with it. So I think in fairness we have to look to other plausible and reasonable explanations. And it seems that we feel that somehow that throughout this trial we have been we have been sort of trying to defend a moving target. That's our impression; perhaps we're wrong. But I think that's how it's been. And I just want to read one last part of our -- from our final brief which goes to the evidence and the evaluation of evidence. This is on page 96, paragraph 180. And I quote from Colonel Jelac trial judgement where it says: "While evidence of a number of different circumstances when taken in combination may point to the existence of a particular fact upon which the guilt of the accused depends because they would usually exist in combination only because a particular fact did exist, the Trial Chamber and Colonel Jelac stress that such a conclusion must be the only reasonable conclusion available." We ask you, Your Honours, to be extremely careful. As you see, we have all these documents. This is part of our dissection of the Prosecution's final brief. We -- I need two or three days to go through them; obviously we don't have the time. But in light of that, we do ask you to look at their brief very carefully, to look at the footnotes, to look at what they cite. Because sometimes as I pointed out they will cite something in the middle of the sentence and not give it context. I think that's important. Where I practice in my jurisdiction, judges would not tolerate that but juries would tolerate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. He's going back into the area that he's worst at, and I just don't think it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just mentioned what my judges would do to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, in your jurisdiction your judges wouldn't allow you into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have heard about that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the Prosecutor needs to learn how to behave himself, and I think those comments are terribly unhelpful. He should be experienced enough to know how to restrain himself and it is disappointing that he is behaving in this way. In any event, let me just conclude by saying that what happened in Srebrenica was a terrible, terrible incident, and I don't think that we ever tried to minimise it. We ask you to consider all of the evidence, be fair to Mr. Blagojevic. Even if perhaps I as his lawyer have sometimes tested the patience of the Court, because I think he deserves that which the Prosecutor was never willing to give him: A fair opportunity to have all the evidence looked at carefully. Because in my opinion, the Prosecutor began with their mind made up when they indicted. And only after that they began looking for the evidence. And sometimes they've put their blind eye to the microscope and to the telescope. And I'm sure I'm going to have to respond tomorrow. But just in the event I may not need to, I just want to thank at this time everybody that has made it possible, the booths, the court personnel here, and the Defence team. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Karnavas. Well, you finished your closing argument within the time of yours. But still we have to stick to the timetable I have announced. So we'll resume tomorrow morning beginning with Mr. Stojanovic's closing argument, and in the afternoon we have the rebuttal and the rejoinder. We might have an extra sitting in the afternoon; it depends on how much time we need. So if there is nothing else for today's session, I believe the hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
